A lie begets a lie till they come to generations. It is human to err, but diabolical to persevere in error. A man that breaks his word bids others be false to him. If the boys don't kiss the misses, then the girls will Miss the kisses. Alms-giving never made any man poor, nor robbery rich, nor prosperity wise. Marks on tables caused by hot dishes may be removed by kerosine rubbed in well with a soft cloth, finishing with a little Cologne water, rubbed dry with another cloth. "Who is that handsome young man standing ov r there ?" inquired an old gentleman of a rich old lady at a party. "That's my son-in-law. He's a leery brilliant young man—made a large fortune by the law." n- deed !" said the old gentleman. "How's that?" "The law made him my daughter's husband." Harriet Martineau was apt at a retort. A lady once said to her, "Women ought to attend to their little duties and let public affairs alone." She replied— " Those who perform their great duties best are most likely to perform their little duties best." "Oh, cer- tainly," assented the lady; "but SORIA women think they have missions to perform on earth; if I felt so, I think I ought to be sent to Bedlam." Miss Martineau answered, "It appears to me that those who think they have no mission to perform on earth ought to be sent to Bedlam." A kindly old lady was cross-examining a class of Sun- day scholars some time ago. She sought to impress upon her youthful audience the importance of maintaining through life a good name, and reminded them that Solomon had declared a good name to be better than riches. "Now, boys, tell me what you would rather have when you grow up to be men. And please think before you answer." lip; came several hands; but the first one called stopped any further inquiry. "Please ma'am," shouted the little urchin, "I'd rather hae whiskers." Monsieur Biossi, a contemporary of Voltaire, wrote a great number of pieces for the theatre, most of which were so loosely written that they were compressed by the performers into farces or pieces of one act. Biossi was much hurt at such treatment, and one day when a full piece of his was cut down from three acts to one he could no longer refrain. " ZoundS, gentlemen," he cried, "if my plays are to be hacked and hewed in this manner, what shall I do to have a piece represented in five acts?" Voltaire, who was behind the scenes at the time, replied, "Write it in eleven, and perhaps you may succeed." WAITING FOR THE BRIDE.—The thoughts of a bride- groom, as he awaits at the altar the arrival of his bride, may be supposed by the romantic to be filled with sub- limity and rapture, while, if the truth were known, in most cases they run something like this:—" Now, where's Emily? I thought she was to come in at the church door as I came out of the vestry; of course, brides are generally late, but she made me a promise to be punc- tual. I don't doubt the best man has got me out here a full fifteen minutes too soon. That is what the matter ; well, at least he has got to stand it as well as I. What a lot of people ! all looking at me, of course, to see how I appear! I declare, I have a lively feeling for the lion in the circus show. There, I caught Mrs. Blenkin- sop's eye; I suppose I musn't bow. But where am Ito look and not catch people's eyes? Emily, Emily, the first thing I do after we're married will be to teach you punctuality. I think it must be twenty minutes since I came out here. There's an awful draught from the vestry door, and there is the best man sneezing. Hang it! what does he do that for? Every one is laughing. Seems to me the people are smiling at me too I wonder if there is anything wrong about me? My cillar is awfully uncomfortable; perhaps it has got unbuttoned behind and is riding up over my coat. I don't like to put up my hands and feel; I'll nod my head and perhaps the thing will settle into place. Gracious! there is Mrs. Blenkinsop nodding, too; she thought I bowed to her this time. • Heavens! if Emily don't come in about a second I shall begin to wish I had never started to go through this sort of thing. There's Rose Mathews; I used to be a good deal of spoons on her once; see her laugh! Of course, it is at the figure I cut up here; now she is whispering—she is looking mighty pretty; I wonder if she would serve a man this way? What in the world shall I do with my hands? The best man has his behind him; it looks rather easy and graceful. I'll try that; but here, we can't stand here just alike, like the Siamese twins. The Rector has his hands in front; I'll see how that goes; it won't do, it's more awkward than ever. No Emily vet! I'll read over the commandments behind the altar. Well, I shall break the third one in just a minute; and as for the fifth, I certainly shall not honour my parents-in-law for bringing Emily up no better than this. I'll read the fourth; it's a long one, and will distract me quite a while. (Best man pinches him.) What is the matter? Oh. the bridal party at last! Now if I don't mistake one of the bridesmaids for the bride!" (But he doesn't, and the service begins.) AN OvsTER STorrir.—" There is one little spot," says the author of the entertaining but veracious little work quoted before, "on the shores of Cornwall which I cannot pass over, because from it came one of the colonies on the banks of the Thames from which the Whitstable boats still draw their annual supply. Into Mount's Bay, the Flelford river, upon which stands the little town of Helstone, empties itself, opposite Mount St. Michael's, into the sea, and in the estuary of that little river, a person of the name of Tvacke, within the memory of the 'oldest inhabitant,' rented certain oyster-beds, famous among Cornish gourmets for a breed of oysters, which, it is said, the Phmnician,, a long time ago,' had dis- covered to be infinitely preferable to the watery things they got at home. These fielford oysters are regularly brought to London. . . . Determined to make his venture, Tyacke loaded a fishing-smack with the best produce of his beds, and coasted along the southern shores, till passing round the Isle of Thanet he found himself in the mouth of the Thames. Little did the elated oyster-dredger think that mouth would:swallow no the whole of his cargo; but so it came to pass. It had long been evident to those on board that oysters which travel, no less than men, must have rations:allowed on the voyage, if they are to do credit to the land of their birth. Now the voyage had been long and tedious, and the oysters had not been fed; so Tyacke got into his boat, and obtained an interview with the owner of the spot when he reached the shore. Be asked permission to lay down his oysters, and feed thsna. This was granted, and after a few days the spores; of ulva latisstma and enteromorpha and of the host of delicate fibrous plants which there abound, and all of which are the oyster's delight, made the whole green and fat, and in the finest condition for reshipment. Four days, it is said, will suffice to make a lean oyster, on such a diet, both green and plump; and Tyacke, joyful at the im- provement which he daily witnessed, let his stock feed on for a week. It was towards evening that he bethought himself, as the tide was out, that if he meant to' reach Billingsgate by the next morning, it would be wise to re-ship his oysters before turning in for the night. The boat was lowered; but as he attempted to land, he was warned off by the owner of the soil, who stood there with several fierce-looking fellows, armed with 'cutlasses and fowling-pieces, evidently anticipating the Cornishman's intention, and determined to frustrate it at all hazards. What do you want here?' he asked of Tyacke. 'The oysters I put down to feed,' was the reply; they were placed there by your permission, and now I am anxious to re-ship them to be in time for to-morrow's market' 'True,' replied the Kentishman, gave you leave to lay down the oysters and feed them, but not a word was said about re-shipping them. Where they are, there they stay; and if you persist in trespassing, I shall know what to do.' Poor Tyacke found himself very much in the predicament of many a fiat who has been picked up by a sharp. A century ago law was not justice, nor jus- tice law. Perhaps it may not be so even now, and the story of the lawyer who ate the oyster in dispute, and gave each of the disputants a shell, may hold as good in our day as it did in that when the author of the' Beg- gars Opera 'put it into verse."—The Sea: its Stirring Story of Adventure, Peril, and Heroism. Mr. Thomas Cook, the veteran tourist agent, is erecting a block of almshouses and a mission hall Tor the use of the poor of his native village, Mel- bourne, in Derbyshire. The buildings, which will shortly be opened, are to be named" The Melbourne General Baptist Memorial Cottages and Mission Hall."

A remarkable breach of promise case will shortly occupy a judge and London special jury. The plain- tiff, whose grandfather is a baronet, and whose uncle is an admiral, seeks to recover £25,000 damages from the defendant, a gentleman of sonic means and of mature age, and part proprietor of a matrimonial newspaper.

Mr. Andrew Carnegie has just passed throngh hii native town of Dunfermline on the way to his Highland Castle of Cluny. He looked in to see how the free library was getting on, aud gave a donation of £2OO to be spent on books and American, maga- zines at once. Mr. Carnegie incidentally remarked that the library endowment was secured by will.

Mr. Howard yincent is absurdly urging the First Lord of the Treasury to provide a man-of-war to take members of both Houses of the Legislature to Heligoland, so that prior to the introduction ,of the Bill confirming the agreement with Germany they may have an opportunity of personally satisfying themselves of the value or otherwise of the island.

All the best constitutional lawyers were, we be- lieve, consulted by Mr. Peel as to the legality of the ear-marking "proposals of the Government, and they decided that the scheme was utterly un- constitutional. The fact that Mr. Goschen should have proposed such a way out of the difficulty has sunk his Parliamentary reputation even lower than it was before.

Sir Peter Edlin must take a back seat. Mr. Warry, .Q.C., has out Edlined him entirely. On Tuesday Charles Jones, in company with James Arnold, was convicted of picking a young woman's pocket. The amount stolen was a purse containing 2s. 4d.. and the amount which Mr. Warry, Q.O , thinks a proper punishment for this theft is ten years' penal servi- tude. Sir Peter Edlin's record contains nothing to brat this.

M. Alexandre Jacques, a Frenchman, commenced a forty-two days' fast at the Royal Aquarium on Saturday, with the object of out-fasting Succi iy two days. "I got a great fight on me," he said on starting the absurd exhibition, but before the end he may come out a melancholy Jacques. There is a limit to the public interest in fasting, as there is in the performance itself. If this sort of thing goes on Succi and Jacques should start level and try which one can starve to death first.

The social reform wing of the galvation Army prooose to enter deeply into a crusade against sweating. A labour bureau, with temporary head- quarters at 36, Upper Thames-street, has been opened,which deals especially with that class of labour termed" unskilled." The Army have issued an appeal to masters for orders of all kinds of poorly paid labour. The bureau is to charge a halfpenny in the shilling, to go towards a scheme of hiring tools, no profit being expected for the work.

It was cruel for the Government, and unfair to their friend Bung, just to withdraw the Compensa- tion Clauses as the "monster petition" was being carted into the House. There were five miles of it, and its weight—avoirdupois—was enormous. And to think that all this length and weight was usless ! and all the trouble which the publicans took in getting their patrons, when in a state of semi- intoxication, to sign it gone for naught. Old Friend Smith should not treat his good friend the brewer thus.

The Australian cricketers, it is stated,do not take their defeats with good grace. Some excuse may be made them, for the reason that they came t) this country not for the love of the game so much as to make money. and the prospects of the tour from a financial point of view are sure to have been seriously affected by the series of reverses they have sustained. All the same, Englishmen are not likely to pardon them for wholesale charges of un- fairness against the umpires who have judged the game. This is not the way to increase their popularity.

One of the most amusing things now in the Nouse of Commons is to compare the different accounts given as to the origin of the Licensing Bill. Mr. Goschen was at first credited with its paternity ; and then cynic Liberals asked the Tories how they could ever expect to be properly led by a gentle- man of German extraction. The daily growing pallor of Mr. Gosch en's complexion—that exasperation of his speeches—the long face with which he has watched the diminishing majorities of the Govern- ment—all these things seemed to point to him as the first and chief author of all the mischief.

But information has varied, and the chief respon- sibility is now shifted] on to the shoulders of the "pompous ass "—reminiscences of the ,Brighton election will recall Dizzy's famous description to Sir Robert Peel of Mr. Ritchie. The success he had with his Local Government Bill turned his silly head, and encouraged him to hope that any other measure connected with local Government, which would be honoured by his sponsorship, would be equally sure of success. He is so dull a man that 'such miscalculation is intelligible in his case. There- fore it is that the Tories, who used to be swearing at Goschen, have now transferred their ,blasphem- ings to Ritchie.

The decay Of the tea trade in China, owing to the constantly ixicreasing preference for Indian and Cey- lon teas, not only in England, but in our colonies and the United States, is producing disastrous, effects in the once flourishing port of Foochow. The native merchant cannot afford to spend so much on articles of dress and luxury as he formerly did; the artisan cannot find employment for his workmen, who, during previous tea seasons, were busily occu- pied in making, lining, and decorating tea chests and boxes; the boatmen and coolies cannot find work, only half of them being now required for shipping off the tea.

A Dublin lady has set up a house for destitute eats, and takes in boarders of the feline race when their own families leave town for a stay by the sea or a run on the Continent A lady who lately visited the home reports that some of the cats have satin cushions, with their monogram embroi- dered in the centre. One pussy has a silver saucer. It may be doubted if she is any the happier for it. Others have separate rooms, apart from the other boarders. They may be of quarrelsome disposition, or possibly of a reserved and haughty tempera- ment, which impels them to "keep themselves to themselves," in the manner of other boarders who are bipeds.

An extraordinary incident is reported from the county court of Wexford. A Coercion Court sen- tence of three months' imprisonment on the usual charge of "conspiracy," came before Judge Darley on appeal. The ground of appeal was that the case was one of mere police suspicion, and, to rebut this, evidence was called as to character. Hereupon the judge produced a letter written to him by one Lord Courtown—a neighbouring landlord, in hot water, of course, with his tenants—discussing the merits of the case, giving the defendant a good character, but insisting that he deserved his punish- ment. In England, we hope, such a letter, if such a letter could be written, would be treated as the grossest contempt of court. In Ireland, the judge reads it with approval from the bench, and apparently acts upon it. Law and Order again 1 . _

Signor Arrigo, who has been interviewed by a Palermo reporter, seems to believe that if the authorities had been more active they might have surprised the brigands during a halt of six hours which they made with him at the foot of Mount Calogero. There they took off their carabineer uniforms, and then led their prisoner to the grotto in the mountains, which was a kind of well in two stories, in the lower part of which Signor Arrigo was confined. In the upper part was the guard, which was changed at intervals. Soldiers and police ranged the mountain, but never found the hiding place. In spite of much suffering Signor Arrigo, who is a tall, robust, energetic man, about fifty years old, is in good health. Another case of brigandage is reported from Turkey. Mabmud Bey, a wealthy Turk, has been taken prisoner by robbers in a northern province, and twelve thousand pounds are asked for his ransom. Bodies of military have been sent to pursue them.

The Rev. Charles A. Berry, minister of th 6 Con- gregational Church, Queen-st., Wolverhampton, has declined an invitation, recently received, to the pastorate of Westminster Chapel, London, at a stipend of over £l,OOO a year. Westminster Chapel was long associated with the ministry of thB late Rev. Samuel Martin. It will be remembered that Mr. Berry was invited a few years ago to succeed the late Rev. Henry Ward Beecher.

German birds are as odd as English ones in their housekeeping arrangements. At the goods station of Jessen a little wagtail has 'this year bailt her nest, choosing a chest in a goods waggon. The bird deposited four eggs, and remained firmly fixed in lager till she had hatched her young. The waggon made from six to eight journeys a day ; but the bird was in no way incommoded, and remained in fall possession of her nest through all the bustle of the service. When a stoppage was made at the end of journey, she quietly fed her young.

"Truth" says:—The only ground on which I seriously regret the cession of Heligoland is that it would in a year or two's time have supplied at once a title and a territory for Prince Henry of Battenburg. "Duke of Heligoland" would not only have sounded well, but,the Duke might have been made governor at the first vacancy, to the satisfac- tion of all parties. If, after all, it had been thought desirable to cede the island the Germansmiuht have been induced to take over the Duke too, and that would have been much to soften the blow.

Mr. and Mrs. deorge Augustus Sala entertained Mr. Stanley at dinner, last Monday evening, attheir flat in Victoria-st. The guests inchtded the Hon. Mrs. Jeune, Mrs. Edward Lawson, Miss Matilda Levy, Miss Dorothy Tennant, the Hen. Lewis Wing- field, Mr. Montagu Williams, Mr. Wemyss Reid, and Dr. and Mrs. W,H. Russell. Unlike the generality of " Stanley "dinners, there was no crowded recep- tion given aft,erwards for scores of people to come and gaze at the lion of the season, as Mr. Sala wanted
to give his old friend all to himself. Naturally two such brilliant and travelled men, meeting after so long a separation, had much to say to one anGther.

div.head: For lonely is the night, and still,
div.p: For lonely is the night, and still,
And, save my own, no breath I hear; No other mind, no other will, Nor heart, nor hand, is near.
Thy waywardness what prayer can move? Can'st thou by any lure be bought? Or art thou, then, like woman's love, That only comes unsought?
! Where's my dressing-gown? My pipe is here, Slumber be hanged! Now for a book and beer. —From" Pirated Poems."
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 2.8, 1896.

div.head: HOW TO WIN ELECTIONS.
div.p: HOW TO WIN ELECTIONS.
LIBERAL PROSPECTS IN NEWTON DIVISION.

The announcement that a candidate in the Liberal interest may be expected to appear before the electors in Newton Division in the course of the next few weeks, has given rise to a general interest in the prospects of the Liberal party in the electoral struggle which cannot be much longer delayed. Mr. P. M. Campbell, the genial and energetic registration agdlit fOr the Liberal party in the Newton Division, upon whose shoulders has devolved the important work of registration, attended by many difficulties of which few members of the party are aware, has prepared an instructive paper on " How to win the Newton Division," which deserves the most careful consideration of not only the Liberal leaders in this part of ,the country but of every individual who is allied to the Liberal party. Mr. Campbell, save : An experience of many years as delegate to the Executive Council of the South West Lancashire ' I Liberal Association in Liverpool, and the past four years as agent for the Newton Division, suggests the inquiry whether the present form of Liberal organisation is best adapted to the needs of a demo- cracy. The question has been forced upon attention by the results of the last two general elections and the bye-election in this constituency. In 1885 we saw the defeat of organised Liberalism in the boroughs only saved from causing.a disaster to the party by the comparatively unorganised Liberalism of the counties; and two years,ago we witnessed Liberalism defeated, if not difiVredited, all over England. Curious results these, of the enfranchise- ment of a democracy -so curious as to call for close and keen study. Of the great improvements made in Liberal organisation during late years in this con- stituency there is no need to speak. They are patent to all who hare ever had to work or observe behind the scenes. A broad, popular, powerful, and adap- tive system has taken the place of the narrow, close, personal, and restricted method of old times, when the popular control of affairs was merely nominal and was directed almost entirely by the selected few. Much, however, could be said in praise of what has been done. But the recognition of progress made should not prevent the equally essential and benetl- cial recognition of progress that still has to be made. The present system of organisation is, in theory no doubt, excellently representative; and where there is great activity in the local party, this may be equally ,true in practice.

div.head: WHAT THE CAUCUS IS,
div.p: WHAT THE CAUCUS IS,

however, often presents an unfortunate contrast to what it shouAd be. In theory it is a central,repre- sentative body chosen by the popular vote of the whole of the party within a constituency and entrusted with the administration of the local political affairs. The method of election is by vote at meetings of the party held in certain definitely prescribed divisions of the constituency—thepoll- ing districts in this di vision,such polling districts and townships returning representatives roughly propor- tionate to the number of resident voters. The bodies thus selected constitute the general associations, the three, five, or six hundreds, &c., as the case may be. From these are chosen the inner Executive Council, with whmom rests the initiative of all politi- cal business generally. Here are the foundations of a widely representative system" The district meetings for the election of members of the associ- ation are intended to secure that that body shall be in touch with the electors generally,and the election of the Executive Council by the general body is meant to ensure their close sympathy with the association ; thus; while all degrees of political thought are presumed to be represented, general harmony throughout the constituency is taken to be preserved. Unfortunately, results do not bear out anticipations. The fault is to be attributed to the local application of the excellent general prin- ciples. This may perhaps be said to .be in some degree hereditary. In the klark days of party or- ganization, the average constituency was ruled by , an individual, or at best by a small baucus of a few personally interested individuals. The broad cau- cus composed of the mutually intrested many,is the lineal but enlightened descendant of the latter. But the "dead hand" of cliquism has never been made to loosen sufficiently its clutch. The subtle force of democratic affinities reqreire that all organisation now should be from the ranks upwards, and not from the leaders downwards. Like the sap in a tree it must ascend before there can be eithergrowth or development. Broad and representative as are the true principles of the caucus system, there has been too much narrowness in their application— too much power has remained in the hands ,of the few. The following sketch of a proposed basis of democratic organisation is intended to indicate WERE IMPROVEMENT IS NEE DED,

and how it may be attained. In speaking of the present system, we are not in any way reflecting upon the conceptive principles of operation of the main scheme of organisation ; we are considering only their effect when viewed with the coloured lights of local application. The last general election may be said to have constituted a supreme test of this local applicaticn of the main principle of Liberal organisation. It was in some respects an unduly severe test. On the one hand the enormous additions made to the numbers of the Liberal party by the extension of the franchise, and on the ether the large number of new constituencies, placed the organisations at a disadvantage. But against this has to be set the fact that an election had been fought on the same register within a few months, the party machinery for which ought to have been equally available for the second and in our case the third contest. In face of these considerations, it must be admitted that the organisation was a failure. It failed as a gauge of opinion before the dissolution, as an engine of education before the contest, and as a means of polling the electors on the day of the election. Nothing was more startling, nothing could be more dangerous, to a party than the contrast between the Association assurances of, confidence and the electoral results of the polling. It is needless to recall the innumerable votes of confidence, as unanimous as they were mistaken, passed by the local caucuses, and notably in the Newton Division. To judge by them, the whole Liberal party in the country had but one mind and one form of expression ; and the amount of Liberal dissentient feeling might almost have been believed to be limited to the dissentient Liberal members of Parliament. It is hardly too much to say that the system collapsed. Nor must it be forgotten, more- over, that the collapse of the summer followed upon a keen disappointment in the winter. The borough returns in November were in many instances a com- plete surprise to the local organizations and a rever- sal of their declared expectations. Those who have been behind the scenes of those party organisations are not likely to have been so much surprised at their inability to gauge correctly the local feeling though I here record my personal opinion that I never expected any of the three men we put forward to

win this Division for the Liberals. We have already indicated some of the reasons for this. The asso- ciations have not been regresentative owing to the principal district meetings having proved unwork- able in practice. Many associations have become more or less close bodies, representative of a few, and out of touch with the bulk of the Liberal party. It has been so common as ta be almost a rule, in ordinary times, for small disftict meetings to elect more members to the association than there have been persons present at the meetings, and this applies to every one of the districts in the Newton Division. Selected lists of names have been put to the meeting, and carried as a matter of the commonest routine. Then, again, there has been a tendency to let the work drift. There exist only vague and superficial relations between the Associa- tions and the electors. The central body takes little or no trouble to ascertain the opinions of the masses. The Association in effect represents, in the time sense of the term, too frequently no one at all but the members themselves. When the time of an election comes, there is a most praiseworthy activity, and the party managers endeavour, with most laudable zeal,to accomplish in a few days what ought to have been, and might have been, the gradual work of .as many years. It is, common enough, in this and other constituencies, to hear complaints of the apathy in the Liberal party, and it is not too much to assert that this apathy is mainly the reflection outside the Association of the indifference, routine, and inactivity which prevail within it. The princi- pal faults of the present system of local organiza- tion are :—TNI non-representative character of the Association, the faulty system of election, the dangerous practice of issuing mere machine-made opinions, the indifference of the bulk of the Associa- tion to the political condition of the rank and file of the party, the want of any methodized system of political education, and the want of any organ- ized method of apportioning work and responsibility among individuals. The results may be summed up in a single sentence; the general unreliability of the organizations, as partially proved in November, 1885, and fatally demonstrated last summer. In contrast to these faults, the ESSENTIALS OF A GOOD SYSTEM of local party organization, as we conceive them,l may be briefly stated:—l. Full, thorough, and close , representation of the masses of the party by the ' body elected to control party affairs. 2. The plainest simplicity of form compatible . with efficiency, so that all election machinery be aim- plified,in view of the strictest limitation of elec- den costs. This, practically speaking, has been the main cause of our downfall as an Association. ' 3. The ability to reach directly, and with a minimum of trouble, the rink and file ot the party ; either for stirring up enthusiasm, getting up petitions, elicit- ing the real popular opinions, or for any other, pur- pose connected with the party. 4. The apportion- ment among as large a number of the party as practicable of definite duties and definite responsi- bilities; ,so that the feeling of direct interest and the progress of the local party may be cultivated among a wide circle. This may be stated in another way as the counteraction of that paralyzing feeling that what is everybody's business is nobody's business. 5. The definite ascertainment by every available means of the political opinions of indi- vidual members of the electorate. Elections, as everybody knows, are lost and won by the votes of those who fluctuate between definite views, and the necessity is great to gain over as large a propor- tion of these as possible. The future of our present system in this respect is evidenced by our confusion as to who are, and who are not, Home Rulers at the present time, and our difficulty in determining the proportion of Dissentient Liberals. 6. The constant keeping alive of an intelligent interest in politics among the rank and file of the party. 7. The main- tenance of the closest touch among all ranks of the party. 8. The provision of a simple, workable, and efficient machinery for political education. This is positively one of the most important of all consid- erations, whether by -already organized bodies or by local efforts like the present one. It would be a waste of time now to stop to consider in which of these essentials our present system fails most conspicuously ; probably in the last or the fourth; and the two combined failures constitute a very grave charge.
(To be concluded next week.)

div.head: SPARROWS' TOWER.
div.p: THE SPARROWS' TOWER.

We take the following from a brochure by Mr. A. Waddell, the sketch being written more especi- ally for the young : April 6th, 1887.—One beautiful morning last autumn, I was walking on the Royal Parade, East- bourne, on that part of it that encloses the "Wish Tower," on the south side.by the English Channel, when I saw a very curious and charming sight. Round the old Martell°, or" Wish Tower" as it is called, there is an ancient "moat," or "fosse," and round that again is a sort of earthwork, such as are used in fortifications. Ido not know whether this had ever been thrown up for that purpose or not, but in the peaceable times in which we live it has been turned into a delightful upper promenade, 'which, in order to render it pleasant and agreeable I to the visitor, has been very Well drained, so that all the rain that falls and might lodge about it soon disappears and leaves the embankment, nice and

dry. Now, there are a remarkable race of little people that, like Scotchinen, are to be found almost every- where, and they have also another characteristic of the Caledonian family, and that is they make use of opportunities and take as good care of themselves as they possibly can. I think I need hardly tell you I mean wee sparrows. Well, anyhow, it is just the little sparrows that I mean, and so they have taken advantage of the drain pipes. Perhaps you never heard of sparrows living in drains before? Neither did I until then—the day I saw them; but perhaps you will tell me that seeing is not hearing ; you are quite right; I always like my young friends to be correct; but then, you see, if I remember right, it was hearing them that led me to seeing them, for such a chirp, chirp, chirping as they made, and when I looked up there were their little knowing heads peeping out of the drains, for you must know that there were a number of small pipes, like very thin chimney pots, and it was through these that tne water was drained away, and trickled down the deep wall of the embankment (which looked quite like a tower) on to the Promenade beneath. Well, what do you think? These clever little creatures had taken up their abodes in them, quite comfortable, and as nice as you like. Now these little birds were not like some children I could men- tion, who are difficult to please and discontented. They made use of what they could get, and did not sit moping for what they could not get. Then, again, they were like the wise man "who built his house upon a rock," and not like the children of Eastbourne, who go and spend their precious time in making towers and forts of sand, which are des- troyed when the tide comes up ; thus the sparrows got their tower, their fortress, all to hand, or more correctly, in bird language, to beak. Now, there are birds called Sand Martins, who ' build in the sand (such as may be seen at Lowe- stoft, in Suffolk), but not where the sea comes up. They are not like the foolish man who built his house on the sand ; but they build in a place which is far above the sea, and also, it may be, out of reach of naughty children who would try to take their eggs, which is a very cruel thing to do. Now, before I close I must tell you a little story about a little sparrow that I found lying on the top of the stairs of Sale station one day more than a year ago. There it lay; it was on its back, and, apparently, quite dead. Poor little bird! its happy little life over; no more to pick up crumbs and dodge the cats ; and two little boys were looking at this poor sparrow. I do not know what they intended to do; perhaps they thought of giving it a squeeze to see if there was any life in it. Had they done so I am afraid they would have squeezed the life out of it. But just while they were looking I came up the stairs and looked, too, and saw the little bird, and very carefully I lifted it up, for I remembered that if it was dead that God knew of its death, for He knows when all the little birds die and He knows and sees when unkind little boys and girls catch and torment the birds and butterflies that He has made. I have heard of a man, and be- lieve it is perfectly true, who, when he was a boy, used to catch little birds and hurt them in such a manner that they could not chirp or sing after. Well, God saw all this, and the man, it is said, grew up and had several sons, and they u:er'i all dumb. So you see if we do not at the time feel the result, we will assuredly feel it later on. Remember the words of Moses, Be sure your sin will find you out." Well, I lifted the little'bird very gently, and it was not dead after all. only.stunned. It had, I suppose, knocked itself against the glass of the door ot the station. Well, I came along with it intending to bring it home. andperhaps, if it would allow me, make a little pet of it ; and the little thing got so nice and warm and comfortable, and, by-and-by, it began

to look about it and take notice of passing event s and all of a sudden there was a sort of little move- ment (I was not holding it very tight, you may be sure), and without ever saying " Thank you," or wishing me "Good afternoon," away it slid from my hand, spread its little wings, and off it went. Now, I cannot say it was polite to go off in that unceremonious manner, but then, you know, it was only a little bird, and had that excuse which rude little boys and girls never have, unless they have not been properly brought up; and besides, it may have seen a friend, an aunt or uncle, or perhaps its own grandmother, and wanted to explain-what had happened. Anyway, if it was pleased, so was I. It is always, my dear young friends, much more real enjoyment to give pleasure than to give pain, and if you will turn to the third chapter of St. Mark and the fourth verse, you will see what our Saviour thought on the subject. He thought it was better to save life than to kill, even though it was the life of the tiniest insect. He, "who went about doing good," He, who called "the little children to come untollim ;" and He who died a shameful and cruel death, that all "who humble themselves and become as little children," "should not perish, but have everlasting life."

div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

"Bloomsbury and St. Giies's, Past and Present," is the title of a handsome quarto volume published by Messrs. Trustlove and Shirley, London. This history of these noted London parishes is from the pen of Mr. George Clinch, of the Department of Printed Books. British Museum, author of "Anti- quarian Jottinizs," &c., and, as might be supposed, it includes historical and antiquarian notes of the vicinities. Mr. Clinch is undoubtedly admirably qualified for this work, and from the care with which it has throughout been done it is evident that it has been with him a labour of love. The volume is rendered especially valuable from the fact that it includes numerous reproductions of rare engravings and maps in the British Museum. There is a striking portrait of the celebrated Eleanor Gwynne, from an original picture in the possession of Mr. Thane; another of the Rookery, St. Giles's, about 1800; and a third of Bird Fair, Seven Dials. There are various maps and plans of St. Giles's, and a plan of the manor of Bloonasbuiy in 1664. The illustrations are for the most part finished in the highest style of art, and have been produced by the London Stereoscopic Company, in their photo- mezzotype process. There' is a very full index, which practically covers every person or place referred to in the work. It should be added that the book is beautifully printed on toned paper, and handsomely bound.

Messrs. Trustlove and Shirley have also published "Norwood and Dulwich, past and present, with his- torical descriptive notices by Allan M. Galer." Mr. Galer has had an interesting district to describe, and it is needless to say that he has produced a most interest- ing work. Re has traced the connection with this dis- trict, of a number of eminent men and in some cases given theirportraits. Amongst the celebrities referred to may be mentioned Edward Alleyn,the founder of Dulwich College, whose career as a noted actor in his day is carefully de- tailed. Then we have references to Goldsmith, Sir Richard Blackmore, Thomas Campbell, the poet, David Cox, Samuel Johnson, Daniel Defoe, Mendelsshon, and Dr. Lettsom. In connection with the famous doctor, it is a matter of course to say that there is a re-production of the noted epigram on his name, as follows :

When any patients call in haste, I physics, bleeds. and sweats 'em; If after that they chose to die, Why, what cares I, I. Let's 'Em. The appendices include lists of chaplains and masters of Dulwich College, with etymological and historical notes on local names. There is, too, an ample index, and Mr. Galer must be congratulated on the result of his labours.

From the same firm we have "Quaint London," a little work by "Old Mortality," who describes a num- ber of interesting relics of old London. Amongst them should be mentioned the Inner Temple, St. John's Gate, Clerkenwell, Tallow Chandler's Hall, Lincoln's Inn Gate House, the Charterhouse, York House and its water-gate, clock of old St. Dunstan's, and last, but not least, Temple Bar. The places mentioned, it should be stated, are illustrated from the photographsof the society for photographing relics of old London, and, as the work is in every respect well done, it is hardly necessary to say that the book furnishes a charming souvenir of a visit to London.

Now that :greater interest is being taken in technical education, a hand-book on" Hand-,ra ft " will be wel- comed in many quarters. This sys,..o of training, has for generations been cultivated in Sweden, and amongst the Scandinavian and kindred peoples. It is called " Sloyd," and written "Slojd," and as the nearest equivalent in English would seem to be "hand-craft "or mechanical training for the hand, that term has been adopted. The book becomes a most reliable basis of technical education in schools and classes, as it embodies a system of pure mechanical art without the aid of machinery. It is admirably explained and illustrated by Mr. John D. Sutcliffe, of the Manchester Recreative Evening Classes, and it is accompanied with an appro- priate introduction by Mr. T. C. Horsfall, J.P. It should be stated that the descriptions are clear and definite, and, along with the illustrations, leave nothing to be desired in the way of clearness. The work is published by Messrs. Griffith, Farren, and Co., London, at 2s. 6d., and there is every prospect of its becoming a standard text-book. The" Life of Jane Austen," by Professor Goldwin Smith, is issued by Mr. Walter Scott in his "Great Writers' "Series. It is hardly necessary to say that this work is admirably written, for Mr. Goldwin Smith is recognised as a master of good English. He gives the main facts and incidents in the life of the eminent novelist, and then proceeds to enter upon a description and a criticism of her various novels. Miss Austen was buried in Winchester Cathedral, and it is interesting as an illustration of the little honour that a prophet has in his own country, that the verger who showed the , Cathedral, once asked a visitor to tell him whether there I was anything particular about "that lady," as so many people had asked to see where she was buried. Refer- ring to eurroundings as sjnfluencing character, Mr. Goldwin Smith says—" There is not a greater contrast between the bleak Westmoreland moor and the soft beauty of the Hampshire valley than there was !set wren the youth of the authoress of Jane Eyre 'and the author of Jane Austen.'" This mention of Westmoreland I moor is an error, for Haworth, where Charlotte Bronte lived, and the moors that she _laved, are in Yorkshire. The work may be said to come at a time when there is need for re-calling and re-reading the excellent novels Miss Austen wrote. We have received from Messrs. Warne and Co. two volumes of their "Star Series" of stories. The first, "A Titled Maiden," is written by Caroline Atwater Mason, and deals with the career of a farm girl, who eventually passed through college, and took the title of doctor. The story is capitally written, there is plenty of weil- defined character-sketching, and the love element is of a kind to sustain the interest from beginning to end. "A Titled Maiden" is an altogether well-written and whole- some story. "My Lady Nell" is by Emily Weaver, and it deals with life in England some 300 years ago. There is a chapter devoted to "Yule-Tide Revels," some ac- count of Oxford, and of the way in which the belief in witchcraft operated upon all classes at that period. The quaint language of our forefathers is well preserved, and the story is throughout connected and interesting. We have also received a copy of a brochure published for private circulation, by Mr. Alexander Waddell, of Sale. It bears the title of "A Bird of the Air, and a Grain of Sand." Mr. Waddell has an aptitude for des- cribing incidents in his experience, and revealing their relation to the teachings of Scripture. Indeed, his familiarity with the Scriptures is really remarkable. We re-produce in another column a sketch called " The Sparrow's Tower," written more especially for the young.
CARDINAL MANNING AND THE QUESTION OF 'PRECEDENCE.

Lord Salisbury has sent the following reply to the Rev. Dr. Preston, vicar of Holy Trinity, Run- corn; who asked him if the sanction of the Crown had been obtained for the precedeßce claimed for Cardinal Manning

Foreign Office, June 21, 1890. Sir,—l am desired by Lord Salisbury to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 15th inst., id which you inquire as to the accuracy of the report that "Mr. Gladstone, with the concurrence of Lord Salisbury, recommended the Queen to place Cardinal Manning's name after that of the Prince of Wales, and before that of the present Premier." I have to say that the above report, in so far as it regards Lord Salisbury, is without foundation.—l am, sir, yours obediently, &ROMBERG MTONNELL.

div.head: CHAPTER VCNIV AN ANNOUNCEMENT.
div.p: CHAPTER VCNIV AN ANNOUNCEMENT.

MARK followed the warder through the chilling white- washed passages, feeling but little interest in what he looked upon as some part of prison routine. He thought once that may be it was to tell him that he was to be removed to one or other of the great con- vict establishments, but his knart was so full of his newly-awakened love, that he felt no surprise until he found himself ushered into the governor's private office, bo stand in face of a stern, grey, elderly man of military port, and quick, sharp speech. and whose keen eyes rested upon him for a few moments in a searching look. "You need not wait, Edwards," he said; and the warder saluted, and left the room. "Mr. Woolford," said the governor. "Air. Woolford." Mark recalled that he was only number forty-nine now. His identity with the outside world was for the present clashed. "Mr. Woolford, I have learned from the senior warder of the extremely painful interview you have lately had, and of the young lady's illness. You will be relieved to know that she is better, and with my wife." "God bless you!" said Mark, huskily. He could say no more, but bit his lip to restrain his emotion. There was a short pause, and the governor turned over two or three papers before continuing. "Mr. Woolt,rd, ' he said; "this is not official, but yours is.a very pec&liar case. I have something to say to you." "If it is to tell me that I am to go to one of the convict prisons at once, I can bear it, sir. I thank you for your kindness to Miss Lister.'' "No," said the governor, "it is not that; and, perhaps, I am going beyond my tether in telling you now, but governors of prisons have a humane side, sir. I sat through your trial, and heard every word. The case interested me." Mark bowed. "Mr. Woolford, you kept something back." Mark started, and looked keenly in the governor's face. "Now, Mr. Woolford, I have a sad piece of news for you." Mark took a step forward, and, with an anguished look, exclaimed: "You told me that she was better." "The lady who came to see you, Mr. Woolford, is better. But I have other news for you." "Other news, sir P' "Yes. Can you bear it? "Bear it !" said Mark, with a sad smile. "air, I think I have been schooled to bear anything now." "I have to tell you of good news and bad news. You shall have the good first." /dark oowed.

- "The fact is, Mr. Woolford, since your trial a good deal hao been going on. A Mr. Klopstock, one of thq witnesses, and a de:ective ofticer have been busy, and from what they found out, they concluded that you have been playing a double part." He paused, for Ma* to speak, but as he was still silent, the governor went on : . .

_ "They concluded that you had been playing double part, as I say, and taking the whole blame to save your confederate. But now they find that you have had no confederate, but that you nobly tried to screen another." Mark's face was like stone

_ "To make a long story snort, sir, I may tell you that it is but a question of time, and the going through of due forms for you to be set at liberty, Mr. Wool. ford, without a stain upon your character." Mark was still silent. "This is the case, Mr. Woolford, is it not? You remained silent to screen another 2"

Mark tightened his lips. "I can see you did, Mr. Woolford, by your looks Sir, you remained silent and bore his shame. Good heaven, sir, it is wonderful! Then we have berms even in these degenerate days. But you understand, Mr. Woolford, you will have to return to your cell." "Yes, I understEnd, sir," said Mark; " but— but —"

"The man for whom you suffered." "Yes, what of him?" cried Mark, anxiously. "It has been discovered, Mr. Woolford, that it it Jour own brother." "But he is not taken?" cried Mark. "Let MI suffer, so that he escapes. I could not bear that he should suffer for his crime."

"He has suffered for his crime, Mr. Woolford." "Taken? " cried Mark. "No, sir; he is free,' said the governor in a low, deep voice. "I grieve to make such a communication to you, sir; but you mast bear it like a man, Martin Woolford is dead—! Poor fellow! he has one through so much, it was more than he could bear." It was, indeed, for as the last words fell upon Mark Woolford's ears, he turned half round, clutched at vacancy, and before the governor could reach his aide, he had fallen heavily upon the floor.

div.head: CHAPTER XXXV.
div.p: CHAPTER XXXV.
THE WEIGIIT OF GOLD.

A mar, foggy evening at Liverpool, with the rain coming down in a thin, almost impalpable mist, and the lights at the wharves and on the great steamers moored thereto looking blurred and thick. It was a nasty night for a start across the Atlantic, but the large packets of the Cunard line study the weather but little, and are well up to their starting time.

There vois a goodly company of passengers on board, and others lounging over the gangway, slippery now with the rain; for, like time and tide, the great Cunard packets stop for no man. The bell was clanging and the great vessel blowing off steam, panting and snorting in her eagerness to do battle with the muddy Mersey, and, like some huge sea- horse, spurn the tidal waters beneath her finny hoofs before going seaward for the worthier adversary, with its long rolling waves. _ .
Passenger and luggage and confusion; lights here and lights there, and highly-pitched voices, with nasal twang, guessing they'd like it better when all this fuss was at an end.

There was a knot of these gentlemen gathered together on the deck, calling each other" stranger," and exchanging cigars and lights, and as one of them lit up afresh, he looked rather scornfully,at a passenger who was passing him. "Guess he'll have to find out his proper place," he .aid. "Niggers have no business so far aft as this."

The passenger spoken of turned round sharply, and darted an angry look at the speaker. He was a tall,well-built mulatto, with very short, crisp, surly hair. He was tolerably well dressed, carried a rug over his arm, and a large satchel' slung over his shoulder.

"I bet his mother was a full-blooded negress," said another; and then they went on chatting as the vessel began to throb and quiver as the great shaft revolved. Then there was a stoppage, with orders and shouting. Another revolution or two. More shouting. The creaking of huge cables, more churning up of the foam- ing water; and., at last, after going ahead and halting, the huge steamer stood slowly out in the dim light of the evening, and floated onward with the tide till she lay lazily about a quarter of a mile from the shore. The mulatto drew a long breath, and proceeded to light a cigar, then he stopped, listening, for there was a hail from a small steamer, which came alongside, and the cigar nearly dropped from his fingers, as some one exclaimed:

"Hallo: Detective, for a sovereign. Some one's wanted." The mulatto struck a fresh match, lit his cigar, thrust his hands in his pockets, and, leaning against a bale of luggage, went on smoking, as a couple of men came on board, spoke to the captain, went into the cabin with him, and then returned._ _

There was a good deal of delay, and the strangers went from part to part of the ship, passing the mulatto two or three times, and then one of them stopped quietly just behind where the half-caste was standing and said, in a low whisper: "Martin! Look out. The police!" The mulatto gave a violent start; and the pest moment a strong arm was upon his shoulder. "It's of no use, my lad," said a stern voice. "The disguise was too plain. Martin Woolford, you're wanted."
"YOU make a mistake, Bah," the mulatto began; but he saw that it was in vain; and in a fit of desperation he drazzed a revolver from his breast.

It was a matter of moments; a few shouts to steno akar; a desperate struggle. "Loose me, or 111-fire !" cried a hoarse voice. "Not I, by George ! Fire away!" A sharp flash, and the report of a revolver; the shrieks of women, the rush of men's feet, and cries for a boat; for, the moment that revolver was St% d, the two men who struggled reached the open gangway, and before hand could be stretched out to save, there Was a heavy splash in the muddy tide. Amongst BO many crowding the deck, it was hard to act, but in an incredibly short space of time, a life- buoy, burning a blue light, was over the side, and directly after a boat kissed the stream, to return at the end of ten minutes with one of those who had gm)

over, leaving half a dozen boats from the shore in search of the other. Then, after a little attention from the ship's surgeon, the rescued man, with a bullet through his shoulder, was placed aboard the small steamer, and taken aslaore, the great Atlantic steamer continuing its journey at last, the lighter for one passenger the less. All that next day, and the day following, divers were at work as near as they could guided to the place where the :warner had lain. But it was hard to tell the exact spot, and a week had gone by before their labours were rewarded by the discovery of the drowned man. For the wounded sergeant bad said, "Keep on, and I'll be bound to say you'll find him. I could swim like a seal when I was young, and swim well now. We went down together like a stone, for be has got a belt crammed full of gold about his waist. I'll swear it was he." And so it proved, for on the eighth day the body of the mulatto was found, the gold belted about him as the officer had said, though there was enough in 'he satchel to have kept him down. For pretty well the s. hole of the money taken from Humphreys' vault was upon his person, the notes and securities so tightly wrapped that they were barely wet, while the di-guiee that Iva° so clever when the passenger went on board, a sorry sham now to hide the features of the WretChea man. wiv but

CHAPTER XXXVI. THE LEGACY IS DEAD• IT was some little time before Mark Woolford came to himself, and then all seemed misty and strange, the words of the doctor who had been attending him sounding far away, and as if relating to some one else. "He'll do now," the doctor said; and as he re- covered he became gradually aware that fate was ill lavish now of her favours as she had been hard Po stern before. kneeling by his side was Ruth, her eyes now beam- fog with love, now darkened by anxiety and dread. With kindly consideration doctor and governor hn" retired, and the pair were left alone to ponder 14'92 the news they had heard—news so full of pain in ineompleteneas,that at last Mark went back to his re° sick at heart in the midst of his joy. For he could think only now of the fact that Marti, was dead, how or when he knew not yet; but there was aterrible dread upon him that be had to Er:aloe:tent misjudged him, and that his brother had ended his lite in terror and despair. Be that as it might, be could see nothing now of _the errors of his brother's life. Death seemed to I'l purified all, so that in his mind there only remeinfiG . the bright handsome youth, the loved one of mother, and the wilful headetrong brother, his lege/ for life. The return to the cell was but a formal matter, fo.r, as rapidly as possible, his case was brought before to? Home Secretary, and in due couree Mark Woolford was free. Time glided by, and there was a dinner given bel., Humphreys and Company to Mr. Timothy Kiopo', . kt which repast he was presented with a testintonitf; and it was an understood thing that his failing heal,. necessitated his resignation of the post of manager in favour of Mark Woolford, Old Klopstock sat very silent till the tiro enlr'd°, when he had to reply, and in the speech he there was something very pathetic, as be terve', Mark, directing his words principally at him. For he said that be felt the honour conferred him in the presentation of the handsome plate, was a proof that he had done his duty to the fjri He should value it, he said, more for that than for?; intrinsic worth. The treasures of this world 0 not concern him much longer, but he ehould l'ke t die respected and esteemed as an honest man I "And now," he said, "in conclusion, I hope. believe, that all here are sincere in wielting me life, short as that may be. I have, then, one r, q )11 to make, and that is that I may come daily to the office and take my seat, not to interfere, but to do as If have done these many years. Let me wear out. you send me to live retired, I shall only die. It came to Mark's turn to speak directly after, for he, too, had received his testimonial, and he spoke uP,:: saying that unless his old friend stood by his counsel and advise, he should feel that the pot fe,, manager was in very feeble hands. And th returned his thanks for the plate that be had receire,; with the congratulations of all upon the fact of ni having taken to himself a wife—the young wife a year after his release from prison, stood with beside a grave in a Lancashire churchyard, whereeo was the inscription— " MARTIN WOOLFORD, aged 25." No word was spoken, but Ruth's tears fell fas,, 55, hand-in-hand, the newly-wedded couple walked sloti away, thinking of the past and erie links it had forg' to join them together more firmly than their marriege bonds, heart to heart, soul to soul. Man and wlle , but lovers to the end.

THE PURCHASE OF THE WATER- WORKS.
ENGINEER'S REPORT ON THE PLANT AND

WELLS. In view of the proposed purchase of the Water- works, Mr. Joseph Mansergh, (Member of Council of the Institute of Civil Engineers, &c., &c.) has reported to the Warrington Corporation the results of an inspection of the Water-works Company's plants, wells, &c. THE PRgLIMINARY CONDITIONS.

Mr. Mansergh says: "In accordance with instructions received from you, through Mr. Longdin, I visited War- rington on Friday, the Bth instant, and in company with that gentleman, had an interview at the Town Hall, with Mr. Nicholson, the solicitor, Mr. Moore, the engineer, and Mr. Ross, the manager, representing the Water- works Company. It was then explained to me, by Mr. Nicholson, in a statement as:sented to by Mr. Longdin, that the examination of the Company's Works which I was about to make, was to be merely a superficial exam- ination; that they were not to be called upon to open out any buried works, nor to Make any trial pumping; that a copy of my report was to be furnished to them, and that the whole proceeding was to be without prejudice. Mr. Nicholson then left us, and the rest of the above- named party drove out to the Winwick works, and we were assisted in our inspection by the man in charge of the station.

div.head: WINWICK WORKS.
div.p: THE WINWICK WORKS.

The buildings li-ire-c.o.Q.s.t-Olai3Oilei:-.house,two engine- houses, and a dwelling-house. In the boiler-house there are three single-Sued Lancashire boilers, 6 feet in dia- meter, and 25 feet long, working at 35 to 40 lbs. pressure. In the old engine-house there is a single cylinder beam- engine the normal speed of which is ten strokes a minute. The cylinder is 30 inches in diameter, and the stroke of the piston 6 feet. This engine drives two singlo- acting pumps 18 inches in diameter, and 4 feet stroke, one of them beirg situated in a well under the engine-house, and the other in a well outside. In an open-ended building alongside the engine-house there is a stand-bye horizontal engine, capable of work- ing the outside pump. This is very seldom used, but is kept in a condition to be put cm whenever it may be needed. At the time of our inspection the beam engine was driving the two pumps at the usual speed, every- thin, working smoothly and quietly, and I had the speed quickened up to 13 strokes without any ill effects on the running. This machinery was erected by Yates, of Blackburn, about 21 years ago, In the new engine house there are two 'single cylinder beam engines, built by Daglish, of St. Helens, in 1882, diameter 21 inches, stroke 6 feet; the, beams being of wrought iron. There is an overhead traveller in this house. Each of these engines drives a single-acting pump, 17 inches diameter and 3 feet stroke, fixed in a well under the house at 15 strokes a minute. I went down this well to the stage at which the pumps are placed, and found them going smoothly and steadily, and apparently in good condition. This well is lined for a short length at the top with brickwork, but is princi- pally left es cut in the sandstone-rock, and is quite dry and clean as far as we went down. At their normal speed the two sets Of pumps will lift just about equal quantities of water. For present requirements, all the four _;'pumps are worked nine hours, and one pair four hours, more in a day; equivalent to working the whole for 11 hours.

THE STEELY OF WATER. I calculate that in this time they will pump about 1,100,000 gallons. Originally there were bore-holes in some of the wells as described in Mr. De Rance's report of May, 1890, but these have been stopped and the wells may be taken as about 150 feet deep. The principal part of the supply is pbtained from a tunnel or heading com- mencing at a shtft on the Company's property and driven in a (northerly ?) direction for a length of 1,227 yards. The level of the invent of this shaft is 38 feet below ordnance datum. At the far end, Mr:Moore said, there was a large quantity of Water, and he had no doubt that by further driving it might be increased to a practically unlimited extent. The water. level ,in the wells is lowered about 15 feet during the 13 hours pumping. From each of the fcur pipes there is a delivery pipe, 20 inches in diameter, with air-v.ssels joining the 24-inch rising-main which delivers the water into the service reservoir adjoining. The reservoir is covered with brick arches and contains 2,044,229 gallons. The roof arches are backed up level, and a floor has been made with side walls so as to contain about a foot or 18 inches of water with the intention of keeping the water cool inside the reservoir. There is also an ingenious arrangement upon the roof by which, prior to passing into the reservoir, the water is aerated, and its quantity can be measured through four open-topped notch-gauges. I could not do more than look into the reservoir as it was nearly full. I measured the quantity that was being pumped by means of the notches and found it to be at the rate of 301.75 cube feet g minute, or equivalent to about 1,244,700 gallons in 11 ' hours. Probably the engines were running a little over the norinfd speed. There is a,little cooling-pond behind the buildings for the condensing water. The old engine has a jet condenser and the new engine a surface con- denser into which there is a slight injection of cold water to prevent undue waxwing of the water pumped.

E1..,6,1T IN GOOD CONDITION: BRANS OF DISTRIBUTION. All the plant appears to be in good condition, the machinery works comfortably, and I see no reason why it should not continue for a considers Ole time to pump all the water that may be needed in the Borough. THE RAILWAY RA.CE TO THE NORTH. The exodus to Scotland begins next week, and the railway companies are engaged re-arranging their trains. The opening of the Forth Bridge has stimulated the *est coast companies, who have promptly repfied by reducing the time between London and Aberdeen of the special Scotch mail by one hour. This is a considerable accelera- tion, as it means that a speed of nearly fifty miles in hour will be maintained throughout the journey from Euston to Aberdeen. The ordinary expresses will a,lso be quickened all along the route, and probably the num- ber of stopping places will be diminished.

REPORT OF THE BOROUGH SURVEYOR. The tradsmen of Bridge-st. have lately been agi- tating in favour of wood pavement for the upper part of the street, which is so narrow as to be often congested with traffic, and in accordance with instruction from ,the Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee of the Warrington Corporation, Mr. Longdin, the borough surveyor, has made areport on the sub- ject which will come before the Town Council at their meeting next Tuesday. It will be seen from this that Mr. Longdin shows that the annual cost of wood pavement is much in excess of that of granite.

div.head: APPLETON SUPPLY.
div.p: THE APPLETON SUPPLY.

After inspecting the Winwick Works, we drove across the town and out to Appleton. These works consist, as you are aware, of a storage reservoir, containing, when full, about 62 million gallons; of a pair of filter beds having an aggregate sand area of 1,000 square yards, and a covered service reservoir holding 350,000 gallons. The drainage area above the storage reservoir consists of two parts—the Appleton brook water shed of 540 acres in extent from which the water flows down its natural channel unrestricted into the reservoir—and the Dares- bury shed of 820 acres, the flow from which is limited by the discharging capacity of a 24-inch conduit with a fall of lin 1,056 ; that is, 399 cube feet per minute, or 4,591,000 gallons in 24 hours. Both these water sheds con- gist of well cultivated lands carrying anot inconsiderable population, and the water obtainable from them cannot be of such a quality as is nowadays considered suitable for general town supply. If, however, these works come into your hands, you can no doubt, utilize them quite satisfactorily for trade and manufacturing requirements and street-watering, sewer-flushing, etc., and for these purposes the quantity obtainable will no doubt be adequate for many years to come. Mr. Ross, in answer to my inquiries, stated that there was a duplicate set of mains already provided in many streets of the town for the distribution of this water. I have little doubt, how- ever, that you will find it desirable to make extension of this system. AN OPINION AS TO THE TERMS OF PURCHASE.

I am not quite clear that lam not going somewhat beyond my instructions in expressing any opinion upon the contemplated terms of purchase; but they have been put into my hands and I have considered them, and for what it is worth I will say shortly what I think. I have had considerable experience in connection with such transfers and am engineer for the Stockton and Middlesborough Water-works. This, you may be aware, was the first case in which powers were granted in the two Houses of Parliament for the compulsory acquire- Ment of the water undertaking by a public body from a Statutory Water Company. This was in 1878. I have little doubt that as you have,had this matter under dis- cussion for some time you may be cognisant of the terms imposed upon the purchasers by Parliament. Suffice it to say that the ultimate capital sum paid to the Company was equivalent to 26i years' purchase of the net income derived by the Water Board in the first year of its possession. Since then money has become cheaper, and in the arbitration between the Windsor Corporation and the Eaton and Windsor Water Company In which Sir Frederick Bramwell acted as arbitrator for the Corporation and I for the Company, £131,800 were paid fora net income of £4,000 a year ; there being £28,000 of authorised capital still unspent upon works. This arbitration took place in 1887. Without going in- to other cases, but comparing the figures provisionally agreed between yourselves and the Company with the above I think that the bargain is on the face of it a fair and reasonable one to both parties."

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE AND THE ABOLITION
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE AND THE ABOLITION
OF SLAVERY.

Mr. Gladstone's attention having been called to a recently-published statement 0 the effect that when the slave trade was abolished compensation was paid to those interested, Mr. Gladstone himself being now in the enjoyment of a considerable amount of " un- earned increment" derived therefrom, the ex-Premier writes : June 24th. Dear Sir,—As usual the statement is all wrong, It was not the question of an expectation of renewal, but of a fall and formal title by law. It was the pos- session of slaves, not the traffic. That was abolished in 1807 without compensation. What the Gladstone family have enjoyed is a large aggregate loss partially diminished by compensation,but the compensation was a noble grant, and the loss wasone which it was their duty to face with- out complaint or opposition.—Yours faithfully, W. E. GLADSTONE.

div.head: ALLEGED ATTEMPTED MURDER AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: ALLEGED ATTEMPTED MURDER AT ST. HELENS.

ATTACKING A STEPFATHER WITH AN AXE. At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Mondays serious charge of attempting to murder was formally heard by Mr. T. Pilkington and Alderman J. Harrison. The prisoner was a young married man named Dennis James Woods, of Nook-lane, Sutton, and he was charged with attempting to -murder his step- father, James Oates, by striking him on the head with an axe early on Sunday morning. The prose- cutor was unable to appear in court. Chief Constable Wood stated that the prisoner was charged with attempting to murder his stepfather by striking him two blows on the head with an axe and inflicting two very serious wounds on either side of the head. Oates married prisoner's mother about two years ago. At half past six o'clock on Saturday night, Oates left the house and returned very late. His wife com- plained to him about it and he thereupon threw his coat, vest and trousers upon the fire. Oates afterwards fell asleep near the table, and the prisoner came into the house with an axe. He dealt his stepfather two severe blows on the head with the axe. About 25 minutes past three on Sunday morning Police Sergeant Brooks heard a loud knocking at the door of his station inSutton-road, and en opening it he saw the prisoner, who said to him : "I have come to give myself up. I have murdered my stepfather. I have killed him as dead as a door nail. I got 'a axe and struck him twice on the head, and left the axe buried in his head. Come and see for your- self." The sergeant visited the house, and found the stepfather with the two severe wounds in his head. There was blood on the table, blood on the floor and blood on the axe handle. The prisoner was then appre- hended and taken to the Town Hall, where he was charged with the offence. In answer he said "I wish I had done as I ought to have done with that axe. ouUht to have killed him so that I could 'be hung. I don't care about my life; it is not worth a button. I hit him twice with the axe on the head when he was asleep with his head on the table, and I went to you and told you I had killed him. I meant doing it, and I shall say no more now. I have told you what is true and short." The Chief Constable added that Dr. Casey had examined gates, and said that he would not be fit to appear far at least a week. Under those circumstances he asked for the prisoner to be remanded for a week. P.S. Brooks gave formal evidence in support of Mr. Wood's statement, and the prisoner was remanded until next Monday.

div.head: – – BRIDGE-ST. AS IT IS AND AS IT SHOULD BE.
div.p: - - BRIDGE-ST. AS IT IS AND AS IT SHOULD BE.

• --- - The Borough Surveyor says :—" The carriage-way of Bridge-st. northward of Friar's Gate to Market Gate is 220 lineal yards long, and contains an area of 1,221 super- ficial yards, having a gradient of 1 in 32. Bridge-st. is one of the principal streets in the town, an owing to its narrow carriage-way combined with a steep gradient,' the macadam of which it is formed is frequently out of repair, and has made the street the subject of many complaints. Although in repairing the surfaceof the road, sand and road drift, and other binding materials have been used to help the macadam to set, still under certain conditions of the weather the stones become loose and dangerous to horses and inconvenient to persons travel- ling on the street. The average cost for repairs to the carriage-way is £22 per annum, or equal to about 41d. per square yard. The question of scavenging is a matter of great importance as regards annual cost on a macadam carriage-way, and I find that taking the average during the year it amounts to 6d. per square yard, or equal to £27 2s. per annum, making the annual cost of repairs and scavenging to the carriage-way £49 2s. In consider- ing a pavement suitable for Bridge-St., the following must be taken into account :-Ist, durability; 2nd, safety ; 3rd, cleanliness; 4th, cost; sth, noiselessness ; 6th, traction. The experience your Committee has had in various pavements insthe public streets of Warrington is confined to macadam, granite and stone setts, boulders and wood. I think the experience gained • will enable you to dismiss the macadam, stone setts, and boulders, leaving the question to be settled wood v. granite.

THE COST OF WOOD PAVEMENT. The question of wood paving, as applied to Warring- ton, is one in which your experience is confined to San- key-street, .which was laid in August, 1884. The cost of maintenance and sanding has amounted up to the pre- sent time to about £lO per annum. Sankev-st. and Bridge-st. are not parallel cases, owing to their gradients being so opposite. In the case of Sankey-st., the car- riage way is fiat, whilst Bridge-st. has a gradient of lin 32. From my experience and observation of wood pavements, and returns received from other towns on narrow carriage-way; and gradients such as Bridge- st., without great care is exercised in keeping the wood blocks well sanded, they become dangerous to hones and people travelling over them. I consider the life of wood pavement in Bridge-st. owing to the traffic being con- centrated on two tracks, coupled with the quick gra- dient, would rot exceed ten yraul§. The cost of laying down a wood pavement, including foundation, would be about £9OO. Taking the interest and sinking fund, to repay cost of wood setts, viz. :—£6oo in 10 years would require a sum of £72 2s. 11d, per annum; and in- terest on foundations, viz. :--£3OO at 4 per cent., £l2 ; to this must be added the cost of maintenance and sca- venging, which would amount to £llO ' • making a total of £194 3s. 11d, per annum; or equal to 3s. 2d.. per, square yard annually. THE COST OF GRANITE PAVING.

For granite paving it would be requisite to have aco Irish or Scotch sett 6 inches deep by: 3 to 3i inches wide,, upon a concrete bed with close pints, run in with asphalte. Experience teaches that this class of material is suited to gradients such as Bridge-st., and would last a period of about 25 years. To render them as noiseless as possible, care would have to be exercised in their preparation, leaving the sides and top surface dressed with a chisel, so thatwhen paved they would be uniform and even on their surface. The cost of such a pavement would be about £9OO. Taking the interest and sinking fund on £6OO, cost of setts to repay in 25 years would require a sum of £36 Bs. ld, ; and interest on foundation, via I—£3oo at 4 per cent. £l2 Os. Od ; to this must be added the cost of maintenance and scavenging, which would amount to £25 Os. Od. ; total, £73 Bs. id. ; or equal to Is. 2id. per square yard per annum. Wood pavement would, therefore, cost £l2O 14s, 10d. per annum in excess of granite pavement." THE QUESTION DEFERRED.
