div.head: COMPENSATION BILL
div.p: THE COMPENSATION BILL

ANOTHER DEMONSTRATION. Anti-compensation feeling in North-East and East London was represented on Saturday evening by a large demonstration in Victoria Park. No impressive charac- ter was given to the event by the formation of a grand proe,ession,butthe various societies supporting the move- ment made each its own way to the ground. Ten plat- forms were provided, and at No. I—that of the London I Temperance Association—Mr. J. Williams Benn, L.G.C., presided. Sir Wilfrid Lawson was the principal speaker. Mr. John Burns spoke at Platform 4, defying the rain, which began during the latter _portion of Sir Wilfrid Lawson's speech, and had washed away the unenthusi- astic fringe. Other principal speakers were Mr. h. Gals- ford Smith, Mr. F. N.,Charringtoe, Dr. Kate Mitchell, Mrs. H. W. Smith, Mrs. Frisk, Mr. W. Abraham, M.P., Rev. Septimus Buss, Canon Barker, Mr. H. J. Wilson, M.P., Mr. C. Fenwick, M.P., Rev. H. P. Hughes, Mr. Pickersgill, M.P., Mr. Morton, M.P., and Mr. J. Branch. The first resolution was to have been put at 7.15 p.m., and the second at 7.45, but the "free wet," as one speaker termed it, having preceded the bugle which should have given the signal they were both put much earlier, and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: ABANDONMENT OF THE LICENSING CLAUSES. _
div.p: THE ABANDONMENT OF THE LICENSING CLAUSES. _

A representative of ti-1-Press Association on Monday evening interviewed a number of representative members for the purpose of ascertaining the general feeling of the House on the subject of the withdrawal of the Licensing Clauses. Mr. Caine said: The decision of the Govern- ment will no doubt enable them to get the Bill through, but my objections remain as strong as before. They have given us a tiger cub and cage to put it in, but we shall have to open the cage when the tiger is grown up. They get rid of the County Council business, and of course they get rid of twelve out of nineteen pages of amendments, which is all very clever, but the fact re- mains that the Government have ear-marked a large sum of money, and have not the courage to go on with their proposals for distributing it. The alteration in the Bill does not modify the opposition of the temperance party ono iota. The principle of compensation for a license as though it were a freehold still exists, and we can only go on fighting. Sir Wilfrid Lawson said—We are exactly as we were before. So long as the Government choose to put in words providing that the money shall be applied to the extinction of licenses there can be no parley with them. That is the whole principle of the Bill. Sir Wm. Houldsworth, in whose name are placed on the notice paper the amendments formulated by thu Church of England Temperance Society, said—We had a number of amendments which are now, of course, un- necessary, but we still have some amendments in refer- ence to the clauses dealing with the suspension of the issue of new licenses, which we shall have to press upon the Government. We do not object to the principle of suspending the issue of new licenses. We desire to see it applied to off-licenses as well as on-licenses. The Church of England Temperance Society would have no cbjection—certainly its Executive would have no objec- tion—to the ear-marking of this money for the extinction of licenses at some future time. Mr. T. W. Russell, whilst retaining his convictions and views regarding the question of compensation—views which he declared were held by the legal advisers of the various temperance organizations in Ireland—regretted, on the grounds of expediency, that the Government had not withdrawn the whole of their licensing proposals, Sir George Trevelyan said—My feeling against the Bill in its new shape is much stronger than it was as originally introduced. The Bill is now, to all intents and purposes, an abstract resolution in favour of compensa- tion, whereas before it was a scheme which we might have amended and made less objectionable. We now set aside this money year after year,and it cannot be touched unless the House agrees to give up the principle of com- pensation, TEMPERANCE MANIFESTO.

Shortly after the statement made by Mr. Smith, a re- I presentative meeting of members of Parliament was held in the conference room of the House of Commena, Sir Wilfrid Lawson in the chair. The followir,ji manifesto was unanimously agreed to: "The so-siied concessions made by the _Government to-niro,-,t with regard to the Local Taxatlon Bill are worse taan worthless, and en- tirely misleading. The Willtransation principle remains untouched, while the "•-•:anfies proposed by the Govern- ment really put OD:,onents of the Bill in a worse ixisition than beferP. With large sums of money hung up, accu- Ml).`,ating, and earmarked for the sole purpose of the ex- tinction of licences, the restrictive and judicial action of magistrates will be paralysed, and any future transfer of power to the ratepayers will be SerionoZ,' fctlei,Td• 1171 shall continue Qne uncompromising oppogition, and call upon those who are supporting us in the country to sus- tain us by continuing the struggle.—WlLFßlD Lewsog, chairman." Trig MINISTERIAL MUDDLE.

The Freed iisociatio-n-u-n-cie-rsta—n-d-s-SK-a-t immediately after the commencement of Mr. Laboucheve's speech in moving the adjournment of the House on Tuesday even- ing a meeting of Ministers was held in Mr. Smith's room for the purpose of considering the situation in the light of the Speaker's expression of opinion given, in repiy to Mr. T. Healey, respecting the Local Taxation (Customs and Excise) Duties Bill. A long and anxious consultation took place, and although in the end an absolute decision was deferred pending a formal meeting of the Cabinet to be summoned forthwith, the prevailing opinion was obviously in favour of abandoning the whole of the clauses dealing with the licensing question. After Mr. Peel's announcement that he could find no precedent 1 for the accumulation of public money in the manner pro- posed, and that therefore the case was one for the House to decide upon, it was felt that the debates on the re• mining stages of the Bill, if persevered with in its present shape, might be so prolonged that after all the passage of the measure would be impossible within the limits of an ordinary session. Both in Committee and in the motion for the third reading, the Opposition would, it is pointed out, insist on exhaustive discussion with reference to the constitutional question, and in neither instance would it be possible for the Govern- ment to invoke the assistance of the closure. Under these circumstances Ministers are reported to have been In almost entire agreement that they had no alternative but to bow to the Speaker's expression of opinion. In the course of the conterence Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain were sent for in order that the views of the Liberal Unionists might be obtained. The Liberal Unionist leaders who had the advanSage of having dis- cussed the political situation with their followers for nearly two hours earlier in the afternoon are said to have held that the withdrawal of the disputed clauses in deference to the ruling of the chair would be a happy means of escape from a position which, it could not be denied, was still environed with difficulties. CABINET MEETING ON THE ABANDONMENT OF THE LICENSING CLAUSES. The Press Association says :-A Cabinet Council, specially summoned to consider what course should be adopted with regard to the Local Taxation Bill, in con- sequence of the Speaker's expression of opinion on Tues. 1, day night, was held at the Foreign Office at half-past 1 twelve on Wednesday, and we have the best authority for stating that the Cabinet unanimously endorsed the view of the informal meeting of Ministers held a Mr. Smith's room, on Tuesday evening, and decided to aban- don the whole clauses relating to the licensing question. A long discussion ensued as to what steps should be taken in reference to the disposal of the money thus re- leased. Several plans were suggested, but it was found that the matter was one requiring very careful considera- tion, and eventually the Cabinet adjourned, a final deci- sion on the subject being postponed. Amongst the recognised authorities on precedure in the House of Commons, it is anticipated that the Govern- ment will introduce a short measure providing for the allocation of the money in a non-contentious manner. In reference to a statement that, in the absence of any special provision on the subject, the money would gs automatically towards the reduction of the National Debt, it is stated that such is not the ease, there being clauses in the bill respecting the residue which would dispose of the money in a different manner. The pubf.shed announcement that a meeting of the Conservative party was to be held on Wednesday came upon the bulk of the Conservative members on Wednes- day morning as a complete surprise, and many hon. gentlemen, assuming that the intimation was official,and that the circulars addressed to them had miscarried,went ;to the Foreign Office for the purpose of hearing the an- ticipated statement respectingpublic business when it was 1 found that the proposed conference had beenabandoned. Complaints were freely made to Mr. Akers Douglas, who, however, disclaimed responsibility for the inconvenience which bad been caused. The fact that the meeting had been determined upon was orally communicated to a number of Conservative members. At the last moment, after the expression of opinion from the Speaker, and the consequent conference of Ministers in the House of Commons on Tuesday night, it was decided to abandon the meeting, and instructions were given for the circu- lars to be destroyed. Mr. Hai-lbwy and two or three other gentlemen put in an appearance at 8, Gresvenor- place, and then learnt for the first time of the change of plans.

FATAL RAILWAY COLLISION AT EARLESTOWN.

A serious collision, which has resulted in the death of one man and injuries to three other per- sons, occurred on the arrington, Liverpool, and ancheqter line., between Winwick Junction and itarlestown, on Friday night last. The occurrence happened on that portion of the line known as the Vulcan Bank, near the noted locomotive works of the Vulcan Ironfoundry Co. A " bank " engine which is used for assisting heavily-laden goods trains up the Winwick and Earlestown inclines, left Earlestown shortly after half-past eleven for Warrington. In addition to the driver, named James Goulden, of Warrington, and the stoker, Mr.Thomaa Young, the Earlestown stationmaster, got on to tbe tender, with the object of riding to Winwick Junc- tion to watch and assist officials who were on duty there expecting the passage of the Royal train from the North. The bank engine proceeded all.right for some distance, but unfortunately, by some means, • the engine was turned on to the wrong line,that from Warrington to Earlestown insteat of the line from Earlestown to Warrington. The engine continued on its journey for a couple of hundreds of yards or so and it then came in violent collision with a potatoe and goods train, which left Holyhead at 6.45 p.m., for Man- chester. The latter train consisted of 28 loaded wagons, and the result of the crash was of a disastrous character. The light engine was completely smashed and doubled up, the driver was thrown among the coals in the tender while the stoker and Mr. Young were thrown on the Jines and rendered temporarily unconscious. The driver and stoker of the potatoe train were alrio badly injured, and with the exception of Mr. Young,who was conveyed to his own_ home, all the injured men were taken to Warrington. Goulden was found to have sustained the most severe injuries, including as they did two broken thighs, and he expired at Warrington Infirmary, on Mon- day morning. The lines for some distance were strewn with the debris from several smashed waggons of the goods train, and five hours elapsed before a breakdown gang from Warrington had got everything clear. The occurrence excited considerable attention in the district, and formed a topic of conversation during the week. Mr. T. Young, the Earlestown stationmaster, though badly bruised and shaken, was able to continue duty until Monday afternoon, when he was compelled, by his injuries to cease work. Dr. Mounsey, of Earlestown, was in attendance upon him and gave orders for confine- ment to his room. Mr. T. Young. the Earlestown stationmaster, has been confined to his house during the while of the week since Monday night. On Thursday afternoon he was still suffering severely from the effects of the injuries he received. He has been under the daily attendance of Dr. Mounc,ey. A general sympathy has been expressed in Earlestown and district for the unfor- tunate sufferers by the accident. The

div.head: POINTSMAN IN CUSTODY.
div.p: POINTSMAN IN CUSTODY.

John Sankey, the signalman employed in the Warring- ton junction signalbox, Earlestown station,vras on Tues- day afternoon, apprehended by Police Sergeant Longworth, of Newton-le-Willows on a charge of causing the death of James Goulden, of Warrington, driver of the goods train in collision at Earlestown, on the previous Friday night. Sankey,who is an old servant of the com- pany having been in their employ for about 30 years,and generally respected by his fellow employes, resides at Winwick and he was formally taken into custody at his home. Later in the afternoon he was brought up before Mr. Gillespie, at the Newton Town Hall. Police Sergeant Longworth stated that Sankey was charged with causing the death of Goulden by causing an enginl of which Goulden was the driver to run into colligion on the railway at Earlestown about midnight on the 20th inst., whereby he received such infuries that he died at the Warrington Infirmar; on the 23rd June. The prisoner, he added, was in cha„Ne of a signal box on the night in question. The deeestsedi nue Goulden, along with a stoker named, *vet, w,ait the driver of a bank engine which shortly before tvielve lo'clock assisted a goods train ttp the Vulcan bank to. Earlestown Junction. When the deceased and the stoker were returning with the engine Sankay through some. cause or other did not turn over the peintsorhieb." I caufecl CicAlden/ (Niue t 9 run (10M the tltille line that they had co& UP Oil. The engine proceeded some dis- tance down the bank and came into 'collision with a goods train. Goulden received such njwies that he was at once conveyed to the Warrington where he died at half-past five on Monday morning. The prisoner kad acccrdingly been apprehended that afternoon, and on being charged with the offence, he re- plied, "Yes ; that was right." He P.S. Longworth) asked fer the pri§oner to ba remanded to the Newton Petty Sessions to be held to-day (Saturday), pending the Coroner's inquest, which will be held in the meantime.— Prisoner vvas asked if he had any objection to azemand, and be replied that he had not,—The magistrates accor dingly remanded him until Saturday, and decided to , admit him to bail, in the sum of £5O, and two sureties of £25 each.

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: THE INQUEST.

Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner for South-West Lancashire; opened an inquiry at the White Hart Hotel, Sankey-st.; Warrington, on Wednesday, into the circumstances of ' thepath of James Goulden. Mr. A. Browne appeared on behalf of John Sankey,the signalman, and Mr. Bland and Inspector Peters were present as representing the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company. Thr Coroner,at the commencement of the proceedings, said that the jury would have to inquire into the cir- cumstances ot the death of James Gotrlden, which occurred on the evening of the previous Friday, through injuries that he had received whilst he was driving a locomotive engine on the London and North-Western Railway, between Earlestown and Winwick. At the time of the accident three other persons were injured, an engine driver, a foreman, and Mr. Young, the station master at Earlestown junction. Passing through Earlestown that morning he (the Coroner) learned that Mr. Young was progressing favourably, and hoped to be able to appear in the course of a few days. Mr. Bland, the solicitor for the Company, who was present, informed him that the other men injured, who were new at Holyhead, were also progressing favourably, and would be able to appear before the jury at the adjourned inquest next week. That morning they would only take evidence sufficient to give a burial order.

Peter Gonlden, of 713, Knutsford-road, Latchford, gave formal evidence to the effect that the deceased was his father, and lived at 14, Paul-st. He was a locomotive engine driver on the London and North-Western HO- way, and was 55 years of age. Elizabeth Clarke, a nurse at the Infirmary, spoke of the admission of the deceased to that Institution, and his subsequent death. The Coroner, after consulting the jury, adjourned the inquect until next Tuesday.

div.head: FUNERAL OF GouLr•m.
div.p: FUNERAL OF GouLr•m.

The remains of the deceased driver, Goulden, were interred on Thursday afternoon at the cemetery at Hill Cliffe. Before the funeral procession went to Hill Cliffe, a short service was held at the Bewsey-rd. Wesleyan Chapel, and was conducted by the Rev. John Gunnell, the superintendent of the circuit. Mr. Gunnell made a few appropriate observations in regard to the life of the deceased, and stated that a funeral sermon would be preached by the Rev. W. Brooks. A considerable num- ber of railway employee's followed the body of Goulden to the grave, and sympathising friends sent many hand- stime wreaths. The Rev- John Gunnell officiated at the graveside.

div.head: OUTBREAK OF PLEUROPNEntONIA. A CATI'LE DEALER HEAVILY PINED.
div.p: THE OUTBREAK OF PLEURO- PNEntONIA. A CATI'LE DEALER HEAVILY PINED.

At the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday. Walter Bennett, cattle dealer. Padgate, was charged with having on the 28th May, at Poulton, acted in contravention of an order made on the 14th Novern- ber, 1889, under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, by causing a cow to be moved from his pre- mises to Latchford, without a license authorizing him to do so, Thomas Oakes, a boy, was charged with moving-the cow.—Sergeant Booth said ho visited Mr. Gaskelrs premises at Latchford, and found a cow which. had Leen sent from Mr.. Bennett's at Poulton. No license had been obtained authorizing the removal . On the following day wit:now went to see Mr. Bennett at Poulton, and asked him if he had sent a cow to Mr. Gaskell's.andhe repbed "Yes." He added that he had no license, and that he was under the impression Mr. Ga.skell'a pro:Moos were in the borough of Warrington. The Chairman (Mr. Gic email) This is a very serious offence. You are moving carats oat of an infectea district intoone whithis perfectly free from disease. The con- sequence is, that through t the length and breadth of the county disease has been sucead, and no end of cows have had to be killed. Simerintenclent Large said he was in- greeted by the Chief Constable to draw the attention A the Bench to the serious outbreak of pleuro-pneumonia in the county. They wished it to go forth to the public that farmersand owners of stock should co-operate with the police in their efforts to stamp out the disease.—The Chairman : Oh, yes.. it is an awful disease. lam quite were the Bench will do what they can to stamp it out, and if dealers M cattle act iu contravention of the Order, they will be severely, dealt with. The defendant: Ex- cuse me. This was done entirely through ignorance.— The Chairman: All 1 dave to say is, that many COUR have • been shmlatered around Appleton. • Sergeant Booth 19 at Mr. Darlington's, 7at Mr. Stmpson's,and 17 at Mr. Knowles's. The Chairman: That is entirely through selling cows, and letting them come here. defendant: TLe We cannot hOp it. The disease sometimes breaks out five or six months after the animals have been sold.—The Chairman : We shall fine you £6 and costs. CATTLE SLAUGHTERED AT CitOVT. The whole of the cattle (numbering eight) at Miss Brideoake's farm, Littletown, Croft, were slaughtered on Monday, in the presence of police officers. These were not affected by the disease.

The Water FOLLOWING upon the geological _Works reports by Professor BOYD DAWKINS,

_ Purchase. and Mr. DE RANCE, on the likeli- hood of permanence in the supply of water at Winwick and at Appleton, a report has now been received from Mr. JOSEPH MANSERGH, Water Engineer, on the condition of the wells, works, plant, dtc. We give it in full in another column, and it will be seen that, like the reports as to the supply, it is a very satisfactory document. The four pumps at Win wick, working eleven hours per day, are found to pump about 1,100,000 gallons, which is something over ten per cent. more water than Warrington requires daily at the present time. The reservoir contains over 2,000,000 gal- lons; and, as the plant appears to be in good condition, Mr. MANSERGH says :—"I see no reason why it should not continue for a considerable time to pump all the water that may be needed for the I borough." As bearing upon the sources of supply, he adds:—" On a consideration of the geological character of the district as described in the reports of Mr. BOYD DAWKINS and Mr. DE RANCE,CtIId the information received from Mr. MOORE, I believe you may confidently rely upon the sources of sup- ply being ample ferall reasonable future require- ments." It would seem, therefore, safe now to affirm that, in the purchase which the Corporation are making, they will obtain a large and excellent supply of water, with reservoirs and pumping machinery equal to the needs of the town—at its normal growth—for a considerable number of years. There is, besides, plenty of water in the Appleton reser- voir which can be used for street watering, flush- ing sewers, and for manufacturing 'purposes. It will of course cost something to bring it into full use, but as to this there is no pressing need for expenditure, and the town will have to spend as it can afford to spend. With regard to the terms of purchase, Mr. MANSERGH, who has had experience as an arbitrator, is of opinion that "the bargain is in the face of it a fair and reasonable one to both parties." This is as it should be; and, assuming that all goes well with the bill in Parliament, the Corporation will be entitled to congratulation on the completion of a transaction which will, in all probability, prove to be an inestimable benefit to the town.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

Considering the sort of drownpour which usually characterises Walking Day, would it not be as well to change its name to Raining Day? However as the holiday folk begin with "heavy wet" it is to be hoped they will be salubrious at the finish.

"Many Happy Returns of the Day" to Mr. Parnell, who reaches his forty-sixth birthday to- day (Saturday). This evening the members of the Irish Parliamentary party are to entertain their leader at a banquet, which will be held at the National Liberal Club.

A resolution was passed at a largely-attended meoting of Irishmen, held in the Free Trade Hall, Manchester, on Saturday, declaring that for Irish- men in Great Britain to neglect registration at the prcsont time, would be "criminal and unpa- triotic." It is to be hoped the resolution will have due effect; and that help will be given by supply- ing information to Liberal agents, as well as by organising amongst themselves.

We have several times suggested that it was not a good thing for the country for Lord Salisbury to be Prime Minister and Foreign Secretary; and now—wonder of wonders!—the "Times" takes up the tale. Its idea is to reconstruct the Ministry, and bring in Lord Hartington as Premier. This means that poor old Smith will have to go to the Hospital for Political Incurables—the House of Lords.

If, as is rumoured, Lord Salisbury holds Lord Hartington's written promise to join the Govern- ment in an emergency, there is nothing for the member for Rossendale but to "tumble to" to the tumble-down Minestry, for there can be no question as to the emergency. He will be able to take some of his followers with him, for, like him, they are "stand-stills." Joseph, for instance, might take office with him. Why should he not go to sleep on the Treasury bench by the side of Rip Van Winkle P

A considerable number of Liberal-Unionists are like Mr. Caine in thinking that the Government have been playing with them in giving it out, session after session, that they were about to settle the Irish land question, and give Ireland local self- government. The fraudulent attempt to endow the brewers has been with them the last drop to an already full cup. One of this class, on being asked the other day if he was still a Unionist said—" No, I am a Re-unionist."

Mr. Caine evidently desires reunion with the Liberal party, and it is be hoped that the way will be made easy for him. Ho has acted consistently in standing by the Government so long as they showed the slightest sign of redeeming their pledges; but he opposed their attempt to endow the brewers in 1888 as he opposes it to-day. He has shown himself as honest as he is plucky in resigning his seat to test the issue; and win, or lose in the present contest, he rises in his own estimation and in the estimation of the public.

It is very disappointing. Mr. Hormuzd Rassam has been searching, with axe and spade, for the site of the Garden of Eden; but, according to his address as given before the Victoria Philosophical institute, on Monday night, he has not only failed to find it, hut has now no hopes of finding it. Ah ! if he had only hit on; and if the garden could have been "restored," as ancient churches are re- stored, and if, as a result, Adam's sons were " re- tored," how very, very happy we should all be.

It is stated that a branch of the Salvation Army is about to en ter upon a crusade against "sweat- ing." The proposal is to obtain orders for all kinds of poorly-paid labour, and enter into com- petition, but making no profit. It is a vast under- taking, and, whatever our fears may be, we cannot but hope it will succeed. There ought to be some arrangement whereby the public should have a chance of knowing and patronising what might be termed the Anti-sweating Shops.

There are signs of a storm in Turkey. The Treasury is always empty,and payments of officials and troops are always in arrear. But just now chronic impecuniosity has become acute ; and, as tho Sultan still continues to give dinners and make presents in big style, the people aro disposed to revolt. Matters are not mended by Russia press- ing for payment of the war indemnity. It is about time it was paid —if it has to be paid. Altogether the shiftless" unspeakable Turk" would seem to be near the end of his tether. The magistrates of Northampton have made a mess of it in prohibiting a public meeting—after the way they have in Ireland. Mr. Labouchere, supported by Mr. Bradlaugh, questioned the Home Secretary on the subject in the House of Commons, on Tuesday evening, and the Home Secretary was compelled to admit that the action of the magistrates was illegal. What holds good for England does not hold good for Ireland, where the magistrates are allowed to do as they like in the way of proclaiming meetings, and using batons to those who attend them. "Equal laws " indeed!

Hood tells us that— Evil is wrought by want of thought As well as want of heart. A sad instance of the truth of these lines was re- vealed at Warrington Police Court, • Monday, when a youth named Albert Saundus was fined 30s. and costs for injury to another bey. By means of a catapult—a very demon of mischief—he dis- charged a stone which struck a boy named France,

who has, poor lad, lost an eye through the injury he received. Parents would do well to destroy all the catapults they can lay hands on; and the police will be justified, after what has happeied, in "running in" all boys who still venture to use them.

It is gratifying to see that great interest was taken in the services, at the Public Hall, on Sunday, on behalf of the Warrington Ragged Sunday I School. The institution is doing admirable work in looking after the waifs and strays of the town. It is hard on children that they should sutler so terribly in some cases from the neglect of their parents; and it is the purest philanthropy to give i them a helping hand n the struggle for existence. The training given at the Ragged School may make all the difference between a boy or girl grow- ing up into a respectable or disreputable member of society.

The officials and the members of the Newton-le- Willows Building Society continue to be all at "sixes and sevens" ; and there is so little pros- pect of a policy being carried out upon which there is general agreement, that Mr. Robert Davies, as solicitor to the Society, has tendered his resigna- tion. Mr. Davies is strongly of opinion that the Society ought to sell the properties in hand, and put itself on a sound footing. There is a good deal in what he says as to the advisability of sel- ling within the next twelve months. The mana- gers may wait longer, and in the end lose more. Time and depreciation go hand in hand.

The report of the Borough Surveyor for Warring- ton on the question of using wood paving for Bridge-st. discourages the proposal—mainly on account of the extra cost. But it is to be hoped that the matter will not be decided at the Town Council meeting, on Tuesday, without further inves- tigation. Mr. Longdin speaks of "returns received from other towns on narrow carriage ways and gradients such as Bridge-st." Why should not these returns be placed before the Council P It is precisely the sort of information they ought not only to have, but to have studied before coming to a conclusion. Wood pavement may cost more, and it may be worth the cost.

I Mr. Joseph Cliffe was summoned before the Daresbury magistrates, on Tuesday, for having his dog "at large on a public place " ; but he show ed that the footpath in front of his house was not public, and the case was dismissed. But this did not satisfy him, for he proceeded to denounce the sergeant who gave evidence for watching him and his house. Indeed, he threatened to put the police officer in the mud, if he came again. Mr. Cliffe does not like to be "shadowed"; but if he were in Ireland the police would Anter as well as watch his house; and if he made such a speech in his defence he would soon find himself on a plank bed. And yet shadowing is "damnable"—as one Tory M.P. has declared.

div.head: 'ME EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 28, 1890
div.p: 'ME EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 28, 1890
TRANSFERS OF LICENSES AT RUNCORN.

The Runcorn magistrates have granted the temporary transfer of the following licenses: The Commercial Inn, Bridge-st., from john James Linton, to William Hulme ; and the Barley Mow Inn, Church-st., from Wm. John McWilliams to Alexander Davidson. BETHESDA BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN. The members of this temperance society had their annual picnic on Wednesday, when they spent the after- noon on Overton Hills, Frodsham. Unfortunately, the weather was very unfavourable, and the greater part of the time had to be passed under cover at Mersey View. The Rev. J. Simpson, the pastor, accompanied the party.

div.head: SUICIDE AT WIDNES.
div.p: SUICIDE AT WIDNES.

Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, on Monday held an inquest at Widnes Police Station on the body of Patrick Derham, aged 48 years, grocer, 35 Alforde-st., who committed suicide on Friday evening last. It ap- pea red that the deceased had been in ill-health for a period of two years and had, in consequence, frequently been ins depressed condition. Flewent to bed at nine o'clock on Friday morning, and he was called at five o'clock to come to tea. As no reply was made, the bedroom door was forced open, and he was found hanging from A nail in the wall, quite dead. The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst temporarily insane." div.head: MAIN OF BOWIS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: MAIN OF BOWIS AT RUNCORN.

A main of bowls (open) was held on the green attached to the Bridge Hotel. on Thursday afternoon. There were about 42 entries, and the entrance money, together with a sovereign added by the proprietor, Mr. James Woods, was divided into prizes. There were a number of War- rington bowlers present, and towards the conclusion of the main several exciting games were witnessed by a large number of spectators. T. Dean succeeded in carrying off the first prize of £2 Bs. from Shay Shaw, of Warring- ton, who took the second of 303., S. Johnson, of Run- corn, was third. Amongst other prize winners were—J. Gleave (Warrington), R. Wright, W. White, J. Johnson (Penketh), H. Gittens, J, Booth, and Smith (Warring- ton). UMBRELLAS RE-007ERED on the premises at J. & W. Dutton's, Sankey-st.—Advt. THREATS AND ASSAULTS AT WIDNES. _

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Alice Ellis, of Dickson-st., was summoned for using threats to Emma Kenyon of South-st. Ellis summoned Kenyon for having used defamatory language respecting her. The Bench ' wound over both parties to keep the peace for two months.—Richard Hughes, of 49 Wright-st., was sum- moned for assaulting his aunt,Jane Simon, of 40 Wright- at., and the latter was summoned for having threatened her mice Jane Hughes. It appeared that there was some feeling between the parties in consequence of a daughter of Mrs. Simon's having been thrashed ; and it was alleged that on Thursday Hughes beat Mrs. Simon severely with his fist, cutting her thumb and giving her a black eye. On the other hand it was alleged that Mrs. Simon threatened to cut the girl Hughes to pieces. The Bench fined Hughes 20s. and costs for the assault and dismissed the summons against Mrs. Simon. RUNCORN INDUSTRIAL BUILDING SOCIETY. The fifth annual meeting of this society was held on Wednesday night, in the National Schoolroom, Mr. John Poole presiding. The report and balance sheet which showed that £3OO had been advanced on appropriation No. 8 ; that the sum of £2OO was lying in the bank waiting to be taken up by the holder of appropriation No. 7, and that there was a balance of £12835. Od. to- wards appropriation No. 9, was, after being fully dis- cussed, adopted on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. John Gates. The following gentlemen, viz. : Messrs. John Poole, James Goodwell, Edward Newton, and Edward Ridge, were elected directors in place of those who retired. Messrs. D. S. Garner and,Toseph Pritchard, the auditors, were re-elected. The Chairman remarked that it was a favourable balance sheet, but it would be far more so if the society was full, and he hoped the members would make an effort in that direc- tion, and try and induce their friends to join. The prospective profits from premiums on sale appropria- tions were considerable, and he thought the society had a good future before it. CRITCHLEY'S Tailoring meets the times. —Ade? .

div.head: SWINE FEVER IN RUNCORN DISTRICT.
div.p: SWINE FEVER IN RUNCORN DISTRICT.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Charles Her- rin,,shaw was summoned for having on the 12th ult.. unlawfully moved a pig into an infected area. P.C. Fryer saw the defendant driving a horse and spring cart containing a pig, past Hallwood in the direction of Run- corn. He admitted that he had brought the pig from Acton Bridge, but alleged that there were not any notices posted, and he did not know it was necessary to have a license. Inspector Bowyer proved the posting of the notices, and the defendant was fined 6s. and costs, 9s. 6d.—George Davidson, butcher, Church-st., was summoned for a similar offence, committed on the 16th inst. The defendant admitted having removed a pig from Kingsley to Runcorn without a license. He said he hired a horse and cart to remove the pig, and when he got to Halton, he discovered that he had forgotten a license, and drove back to the Police Station, but was refused a license. P.S. Gos- ling said the request was refused because the de fendant had no declaration from the seller of the pig.— The magistrates inflicted a fine of ss. and costs, 10s. 6d. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED on the premises at J. A W. Dutton', Sankey-st.—Adrog. ASSAULT ON A BROTHER AT SUTTON.

Alexander Bate, veterinary surgeon, of Frodsham, was summoned to Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, to answer a charge of assaulting his brother William Thomas Bate, farmer, of Sutton. Mr. J. Burton prose- cuted. The complainant stated that the defendant on the 19th inst., came to his house at Sutton about the rent of some cottages at Woodliouses. Witness told him that the executors would see to the matter; but defendant replied that he would have the money then and there, and that he would put the complainant into the County Court if it was not paid. Witness said he did not want any bothQr with him, and defendant, who was riding in a gig, called him opprobrious names, and struck at him with his whip. Complainant's son received the blow across the face. Defendant, who, it was alleged, was not sober, drove away, and got his gig into a ditch, and witness, on going no to him to render him assistance, was struck across the shoulder with the whip. He received two blows, and defendant threatened "what he would do for him " (coinplainant.)—Hannali Bate, the last wit- ness's wife, and Henry Bate, prosecutor's son, gave corroborative evidence.—Defendant said he was one of the trustees appointed under his mother's will, and on the day in question he went to his brother to ask him whether he had drawn the rent for the cottages at the Woodhouses. Complainant abused him shamefully, and he struck at complainant in self-defence with a whip which had no lash attached; but he did not believe that the blow caught the complainant, who followed him, and shouted "Come on, lads; we will fetch him out of the gin, "—The Chairman said it was a very unfortunate thing to see two brothers in court, and the case would not have the effect of improvinr, the feeling towards each other, but rather to make it 7Vorse. It was a serious thing for the defendant to take the law into his own hands, and he certainly ought to have known better than to act in that manner. A fine of 10s. and 15s. costs would be inflicted. A LITTLE RIOT AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Mary Byrom, Ellen Walsh, and Mary Forster, of Walmesley-st., were summoned for having wilfully damaged the house occu- pied by Mary Ant' Murphy in the same neighbourhood. Mr. Knowles prosecuted, and Mr. F. J. Poole, defended Walsh and Byrom.—Mr. Knowles said about a fortnight ago, Mrs. Murphy gave evidence in a case at that court, and,in consequence,a man named Ford and his wife used threats towards her and in default of finding sureties for their good behaviour they went to goal. The defendants threatened that the Murpheys should have as pleasant a Sunday as the Fords would have in goal, and about ten o'clock on Sunday morning, Mrs. Murphy hearing something at the back door went there and saw two or three score of women and children gathered about. Walsh and Byrom were in an adjoining yard. and they both threw bricks at the window. After all the windows of the lower part of the house had been broken, Mrs. Forster threw half a brick at an upper win- dow, and shouted out to Walsh not to forget the top, as she would get no more " time " for it. Altogether 27 squares of glass were smashed and the window frames were also broken. Mr. Midwood was the agent for the I property and his collector Mr. Siddon had estimated the damage at o.—lnspector Keighley said he was fetched to the neighbourhood and found quite a riot taking place and the whole scene was disgraceful. On Wednes- day when Ford and his wife arrived from goal, they I were received with great cheering in the street.—P.C. Cummings said when he served Walsh with the sum- mons, she said she would take all the blame on herself, and make "the old—" lose her costs. In consequence of the disturbances that had occurred he had been almost regularly in the street.— For the defence, Walsh was called and alleged that rude language was used to her and she broke all the windows herself. She was positive that Mrs. Byrom and Mrs. Forster were not there at all and had nothing to do with the window breaking.—Catherine Mulholland and other witnesses corroborated.—Mr. Deacon said the magistrates were quite satisfied that the whole of the defendants were at this riot. The whole thing was a great disgrace to the neighbourhood, and they had deter- mined to fine each defendant 40s. and costs; and ordered the payment of the damage. Walsh would have to pay n 05.).0d. and Byrom and Forster each £3 ss. 10d., or in default a months' hard labour. All the, prisoners went to goal. Mr. Knowles said this was a case in the public interest and he argued that a private individual ought not to bear the costs. He therefore asked that the costs should be allowed. The magistrates agreed to do so. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERF.D on the premises at J. W. t Dutton's, Sankey-st.--Adet.

MATCH BETWEEN RUNCORN BOWLERS. At the green attached to the Bowling Green Inn, Chester, on Wednesday, a match for a stake of £2O took place between Thomas Woods and William Rhodes, of Runcorn. The two bowlers played a game for a similar amount a week previous, when Woods won by 27 points in a game of 101. On the present occasion Woods again alerted his superiority. At the interval the game was called Woods 52, Rhodes 35. On resuming Woods easily held his lead and eventually won by 28 points, the full scores being Woods 101; Rhodes 75.

A FROI7SHAM GENTLERAN DROWNED AT WESTON. Mr. Henry Green, of Barley Grove, Frodsham, strangely disappeared last week end. Formerly mana- ger of Hadfield's Bone Works at Sutton, and recently manager of the Sugar Works at Garston, Mr. Green was in the habit of living At the latter place, and spending the week end with his family at Frodsham. Last Satur- day he did not return hothe as usual, and nothing could be-heard of him on the day following, and information was given to the police. On Wednesday a boy found the deceased's podket book floating on the Weaver canal near Weston Works and subsequently the body of the missing man was recovered near the same spot. At the Royal Oak Hotel, Weston, on Thursday afternoon, Mr. J.h. Worsley, coroner, held an inquest on the body.— James Green, son of the deceased. said his father was 56 years of are. He was a sanitary engineer, and up to his death had been lodging at Garston, returning home to Frodsham at theweek end. Another witness,or Heath- road, Weston, deposed that he saw the deceased on Satur- day night at a quarter past ten. He was walking past Weston Works in the direction of the canal. Wit- ness spoke to him, and he made no reply. He was staggering and appeared to be in drink.—P.C. Breeze said he saw the deceased at 9.30 in Heath-road. On Wednesday the river Weaver Canal was dragged and the body was recovered. There were no marks of violence. In the pockets was £3 3s. 6d., and the deceased's watch and chain were safe.—Henry Green, landlord of the Royal Oak, Weston, said the deceased came to his house between six and seven o'clock on Saturday night and left about nine o'clock. He had three or four " small" whiskies and soda water, and when he left he appeared not to be drunk.—A juryman said he saw the deceased shortly before nine o'clock and he was certain he was sober.—The Coroner said the influence of the liquor might not show itself while a man was in the house but immediately he got into the open air the drink had its effect. He thought the jury could return no ether ver- dict than " found drowned."—The jury returned the verdict suggested.

div.head: NEW MUSIC.
div.p: NEW MUSIC.

Mr. Percy Randall, of Warrington, as will be seen from our advertising columns, has composed and published two new pieces of music. One of them is a Schottische, entitled " Raddon Court." and it is appropriately dedicated to3frs.Reynolds. The other is a polka which. is dedicated to his children Marie and Berte. Mr. Randall composed a gavotte some time ago which was much admired. It will be found that the latest productions are tuneful, spirited and all that can be desired as dance music. The polka and schottische ought to find a reatly sale amongst those who are always on the look out for something good as well as new. SAD COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT ASHTON. _ _ _

An inquest was held before Mr. Samuel Brighouse coroner, at the Blue Bell Inn, Ashton, relative to the death of William Ralphson, fifty-seven years of age, of Rectory-road, Downall Green, Ashton. The evidence showed that the deceased was a dataller, employed by Messrs. Richard Evans and Company, at their Bushey Park mine, Pewfall Colliery. On Sunday night he and two others were engaged fir- ing a bar under a stone in the roof in one of the roadways, when the stone, weighing about half a ton, suddenly fell. The deceased was killed instantly the bar striking him a terrible blow on the head. The others were slightly injured.—The jury re- turned a verdict of" Accidental death."

BANKRUPTCY. - HEAVY LOMB OF Hoasze AND
Cernz.

The public examination in bankruptcy of John Booth, farmer, Runcorn, took place yesterday at Warrington Bankruptcy Court, before the registrar, Mr. E. J. Nicholson. Mr. Forshaw (Messrs. P. Davies and Forshaw) represented the debtor. The liabili- ties were stated to be £382 2s. 11d, and the assets £409 19s. 10d. The bankrupt stated that up to about eleven years ago he was a labourer at Ockle- stone tannery, Runcorn. lie then commenced business in Runcorn as a greengrocer in a small way with a capital of £2OO hie savings, lie after- wal ds became tenant of the Bates Bridge Farm, near lluncorn. which he had occupied ever since. He first became aware of his insolvency when he was served with a writ about three weeks ago, and he suspended payment of his debts on the 10th inst. He had kept no books, not being able to read or write, and he attributed his failure to losses of nine ' horses valued at £202, and eleven cows and calves valued at £144 Ile could give no reason for these losses unless they were caused by the proximity of certain chemical works, which had also damaged his growing crops. The further hearing of the case was adjourned till the 25th July. LOCAL MINERS AT SOUTHPORT. .

A great demonstration of the miners of Lancashire and Cheshire was held at Southport, on Saturday, when that town received an infix of visitors to the number of nearly 100,000, the greater number of whom are miners. From all parts of Lancashire and Cheshire special trains conveyed colliers to and from Southport, and a special platform had to be erected , to cope with the enormous amount of traffic. The miners assembled on the sands in front of the pro- menade, and when all had arrived marched in pro- cession throught the principal streets of the town to the Recreation Ground. Each lodge or detach- ment of the • men was headed by a banner and a band. Between three and four thousand miners were conveyed from St. Helens in three special trains and were headed by the Roughdale's Brass Band, and a large banner, which on one side depicts Truth and Justice holding a pair of scales. while the reverse side shows an excellent painting of Mr. Thomas Glover, the local miner's agent, accompanied by a miner, waiting upon the employers. Under- neath were the words "Caine, let us reason to- gether." The miners of Aehtou and Haydock were represented to the number of 2,500, and with their banners and bands, formed an imposing portion of the procession. An the recreation ground there was a vast: assembly in groups round two platforms. One platform was presided over by the Mayor of Southport ( Mr. A. Pilling), and on the other plat- form were Mr. Robert Leake, M.P., who presided, Thomas Glover (St. Helens) S. Woods (president of the federation), and many ottiers.—ln the course of the proceedings Mr. Thomas Glover (St. Helens) moved the following resolution :—" That in the opinion of this mass meeting of Lancashire and Cheshire miners, the exaction of mining rents aud minirg royalties is a heavy and grievous burden on the mining industry of this country, and we trust that the eutcome of the Royal Commission appointed ta inquire into this question will he the means of removing this obnoxious burden. We also desire to express our strong condemnation of the Employer's Liability Bill, bought in by the Home Secretary,and to state emphatically that no new Employer's Liability Bill can be aecepted by the miners of 'Lan- cashire and Cheshire which contains a contracting out clause. We therefore urge the labour members and others to oppose the bill. Seeing that the representation of the great labour interest in St. Helens is very limited, we pledge ourselves to take this matter up in all earnestness, and assist in re- turning labour members for Lancashire, and as a first instalment we pledge our unbounded support in assisting to teturn Mr. S. Woods to Parliament for the Inca Division." The resolution was seconded by Mr. R. Watts, of Manchester, and carried. GARDEN TOOL.---3. S. Garland, Ironmonger, Warrington Earlestown. PENICETH. WESLEYAN SIINDA.Y SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY. I On Sunday, anniversary services were held in connection with the Penketh Wesleyan Sunday School. At the morning and evening service, Mr. 'John Bennett of Bewsey Old Hall, Warrington, was the preacher. Special hymns were sung at each service by the choir and children, the fourth hymn at the morning service which was taken by the infant scholars, being sung in a very pleasing , manner. In the evening, before the sermon, the first anthem," Ye shall dwell in the land," by Sir John Stainer, was very pleasingly given, the bass solo, with which the anthem opens, being taken by Mr. R. E. Garnett. After the sermon the final anthem" Lift up your heads," by Mr. T. Mee Patti- son, was rendered by the choir. In the afternoon the sacred cantata "The Good Shepherd." by T. Mee Pattison, was given by the choir and children. In the solos, duets, and quartets, &c., the soprano parts were taken by Miss L. Routledge, Miss E. Hobson, and Miss Hughes, the contralto parts by Miss A. Moses, the tenor by Messrs. J. T. Budden • and A. Seed, and the bass by Messrs. 'A. Greenhalgh and J. A. Smith. The congregations were very large, and the collections, which were made after each hervice in aid of the Sunday School funds, amounted to .£25 16s. Mr. W. J. Wigfield was at the organ in the morning and evening, and Mrs. C. E. Parker in the afternoon.

It is from the vigorous pen of Henry Frith, author of "The Mystery of Moor Farm.' "On the Wings of the Wind," "Through Flood, through Fire," &c., &c. Sr. MICHAEL'S CHURCH, RUNCORN. In aid of the choir fundlof this church, the Rev. C. J. Robinson M.A., rector of Halewood, preached two ser- mons on Sunday. There were good congregations at each service, and the choir rendered specially selected music in a most praiseworthy manner. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED on the premises at J. & W. Dutton's, Sankey-st.—Advt. OPEN AIR CONCERTS AT RUNCORN. The Runcorn Volunteer band gave their second open air concert at the Market-place, on Monday evening. In spite of the unfavourable weather, a capital andience assembled to listen to a programme of high class music, which was rendered in a most creditable manner. THE CONVERTED COLLIER AT RUNCORN. Under the auspices of the Gospel Union Mission R. Weaver, known as the converted collier, on Sunday preached two sermons in Runcorn Public Hall, to good congregations. He preached a third s.rmon in the same building on Monday evening, and the whole of the services were of a most successful character. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED on the premises at J. & W, Dutton's, Sankey-st.—Advt. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH WIDNES. The anniversary of the Sunday School in connection with this church was celebrated on Sunday when the Rev. J. W. Chisholm, of Halifax, preached two sermons to crowded congregations. In the afternoon the service of song, entitled " Little Pilgrim " was rendered by the scholars and choir. The narrative was read by the Rev. R. G. Hughes (Congregational minister). On Monday evening, Mr. Chisholm delivered his popular lecture " when you come to think of it." Mr. Thomas Snape C.C., oce.upied the chair, and • there was a capital audience. The collections realised a satisfactory sum. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED OR the premises at J. Si W Dutton's, Sankev-St.—Advt. A SEAMAN AND HIS WAGES AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Police Court on Monday, Robert Allen, an able seaman, summoned Stewart McGiffin, captain of the schooner Bohemian Girl, to recover £3 7s. Bcl., wages alleged to be due to him.—Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, solicitor, appeared for the complainaat, who stated that he was engaged at Londonderry on the 26th of May by the defendant for the home trade, the rate of wages to be £3 108. per month, subject to 24 hours' notice on either side, to be given at any port of discharge. Witness gave the defendant notice at Garston, which was a discharging port, and had asked for his wages in the presence of a superintendent of the Board of Trade, and defendant promised to pay in an hours' time. Defendant had never made any complaint against complainant, who claimed £3 7s. 81.—An order was made on the defendant for payment, with £1 is. costs. VIOLENT ASSAULT WITH A SPADE AT WIDNES. Before Mr. John Brock and Mr. H. Wade Deacon at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Samuel Greeman, of 29 Water-street, was charged with unlawfully wounding John Quinn, labourer of 13, Cromwell-street. Quinn had formerly lodged with the prisoner and on Saturday night, while in an advanced state of intoxication he went for two pawntickets referring to his shirts. It was alleged that, without the slightest provocation, the pri- soner struck Quinn on the face with his fist, felling him to the ground. The prisoner then kicked him with his clogs, knocking one of his teeth out, and as Quinn was running from the house, the prisoner struck him on the back of the head with a spade, cuisine" a Wound an inch and a half in length penetrating to the bone. Two women named Mary Tracy and Mary Reynolds rescued him.—The prisoner, who denied using the spade was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. . div.head: LATCHFORD BRIDGES. ACKERS-LANE BRIDGE ABANDONED.
div.p: THE LATCHFORD BRIDGES. ACKERS-LANE BRIDGE ABANDONED.
[FROM OUR SPBCIAL REPORTRR.] LONDON. FRIDAY NIGHT..

Before a select Committee of the House of Lords, • presided over by the Right Hon. the Earl of Straf- ford, the Manchester Ship Canal (various powers) Bill came up as an opposed measure. Mr. Pember, Q.C., who appeared for the Manches- ter Ship Canal Company, stated that they had for- tunately got rid of the opposition of nearly all their opponents—in fact, of all their opponents except one—and ;he could not help thinking that the Warrington Corporation, for whom his learned friend Mr. Pembroke Stephens appeared—when they heard the case for the promoters, and the evi- dence that Mr. Leader Williams, the principal engi- neer to the Canal, had to testify in confirmation— better counsels would prevail. Having submitted the plan of the proposed works, the learned counsel proceeded to explain that by the Manchester Ship Canal Act of 1885 three swing bridges were proposied at three points where roads were cut asunder—at central points. It, of course, naturally occurred to the engineers that provision must be made for car- rying those roads over their canal, and the first; and most obvious course, seemed to be to el,) so by swing bridges, and swing bridges were accordingly proposed. But when the road authorities in the neighbourhood came to consider the matter with the Manchester Ship Canal Company, and the works came to be carried out, it became obvious to every one that an improvement might be made; and that some of those swing-bridges might be got rid of. They were very close together. lie did not think that the outside two were more than a of a mile apart,if they were as far as that; and considering't hat the canal was to be used by large steamers, the way of which it was extremely difficult to stop, it became almost self- evident that if one bridge was opened and a steamer under weigh was going through it was almost a certainty that if she was at all a large vessel, the other two bridges would have to be opened simultaneously. So that those three bridges would all be open at the same time. The consequences of that would be that traffic going to or coming from Warrington by whatever route, would find the way blocked- by the open bridges, because it would be seen by the plan that there were several roads on the south side converging across the canal towards the same point northwards. The road authorities and the Manchester Ship Canal Company laid their heads together and they came to the conclusion that the Canal Company should make certain proposals to Parliament with a view to improving upon the state of; things originally contemplated. The Com- pany came practically to an agreement with the road authority as to what the new plan sheuld be. In the meantime, however, came the legisla- tion of 1888, and along with it the transfer- ence and powers of the road authority to the County Council. The last-named body had then to be consulted, and the tled to fur- ther negotiations, and the County Council- were not satisfied with the arrangement originally made between the promoters of the bill and the former road authority, but, at last, after considerable nego- tiations, which continued until the middle of this spring, in fact until after the deposit of the bill and after the time when the bill should have been before a Committee of their lordships' House, a fresh settlement was made which involved a departure from the bill as deposited, so great a departure that an additional provision became necessary, and their lordships' Committee were now hearing the bill which was the result of that additional pro- vision. The upshot of the changes resolved itself into this—that there would only be one swing bridge over the canal instead of three, and that per- manently available for road traffic. Now everyone concerned except the Warrington Corporation were very well pleased with that arrangement, and the persons interested were the old road authorities and the County Council. and lastly, but not least, the London and North-Western Railway Company. The latter Company were very much interested in the matter. Their railway—the existing line from Warrington—passed quite close to the canal. It had had to be elevated so as to enable ships to pass under the railway, and that deviation would be observed on the plan at the Latchford new station. The result was that" the London and North-Western Company were getting excellent new roads and bridges which would tend to their new station at Latchford, and the County Council also saw the advantage of changes which he (Mr. Pember) had mentioned. As he had already observed the only persons who had anything to say against them were the Corporation of Warrington. They had presented a petition, which was technically called a petition, against alterations. There were certain other things which they complained of oi the arrangements made under the additional provision. The way in which the Warrington Corporation had, however, drawn their petition, made it very difficult for him to under- stand what their grievances were, because they did not name either the roads or gradients of which they complained. Mr. Pembroke Stephens, Q.C., observed that owing to the method in which the negotiations were being carried on, it was most difficult for the objectors to know the roads with which the promoters were going to deal. Mr. Pember admitted that there was some excuse for 'his learned friend. There was objection made also in connection with he sewers and gas pipes, but the canal had been deg, and they had not found any yet, and if they had they had made proper pro- vision concerning them. Mr. Pembroke Stephens.—l don't think you need go into the question of the gas pipes. Mr. Pember said that he ' had very little doubt that when his learned friend had heard the evi- dence he would find that the Canal Company had wine as far as it was possible for them to go in meeting the wishes of the parties concerned. Mr. Leader Williams, Chief Engineer of the works for the Manchester Ship CanaLwas then examined by Mr. Balfour Browne, Q.C., and referred to the fact that certain works were required to be done in the townships of Latchford and Appleton. With im- perfect consideration of the matter he had thought it only fair to the different highway authorities to give swing bridges over the roads intersected by the canal. He had had, however, hardly time to con- sider the matter. Upon further reflection he had come to the conclusion that something better might be devised both in the interests of the Canal and also in the interests of the public. What he was now proposing would be a great improvement to the canal and did no harm to those who wanted to use the roads. But it could hardly be called his design. It waspartly his design and partly an arrangement with the surveyor of the County Highway Board and the road authorities—a sort of give-and-take arrangement in order to meet their views. Ile felt that it would be no use coming before the Committee without settling with the highway authorities and he had done so. The London and North- Western Railway Company were opposed to a swing bridge at Latchford in case it might be open at a time when passengers were corning to catch trains, that being a residential district for the population about Warrington. The only thing that affected the Warrington Corporation was ,the bridge at Acker's- lane, in which, of course, they were directly inter- ested only as far as their boundary extended. No doubt they were indirectly interested also outside the boundary. Wash-lane would be continued by the new proposed road running along the embank- ment of the high level bridge to the south side, and then on the south side that road was divided into two,'so as to accommodate the people going east and west. The distance passengers had to go along the new road was only 50 yards more than if they went along Wash-lane. On the other hand there would be a swing bridge and the Knutsford-rd. and higii level bridge, in the centre of, and approached by, three main roads, and which would be always open to the public. Mr. Balfour: Can you conceive that that fixed bridge has not servod all the purposes that the War- rington Corporation can have in view and that would have been served by swing bridges? Witness: Warrington is some distance away and as I have settled with the road authorities I think that Warrington interests are well protected; the part that they are interested in is that part winch continues Wash-lane to the permanent bridge. Mr. B. Browne: What are you prepared to do to meet the objection of the Corporation of Warring- ton ? Witness: I may state that the high level bridge I designed at a width of 25 feet, and it has been said by the Warrington Corporation, with some force I acknowledge, that the road approaches to the bridge ought to be wider than the bridge. I don't think that there is an objection to the width of the bridge, but as the road approaches in order to get to the high level bridge are on a steep incline —one in 25—suitable for carriages and pedestrians —they have asked to have•the approaches widened to 36 feet. That refers to the approaches upon the ,north, and I think if I am to do that it would be
nly fair to make the road which rune away to the west at least 30 feet wide.

Mr. B. Browne: Is there anything else you can state that you are prepared to do, so as to meet the objections of the Warrington Corporation? Witness: They have raised the point that the curve under the railway in Wash-lane is somewhat sharp, and it is obliged to be so owing to the osi- tiou in which lam placed by the roads and the rail- way. I have constructed the bridge 25 feet between the abutments, that is in accordance with the de- posited plans as agreed upon at the time of the passing of the Act. But the Warrington people say tbat that might have been sufficient for the traffic of Ackees-lane and Grappenhall-road, or with a' direct line, but now that we are making the high level bridge and making Wash-lane a main road, they propose to widen Wash-lane and to make it 40 feet wide, and they state that a bridge 25 feet wide would be a nuisance. But I have built that bridge and it would be a serious and an expensive matter to pull down the bridge and to put it up again. It means just a little reasonableness on both sides.

If th; Corporation saw their way to accept the existing bridge you would be very pleased? Yes. Bull think r might widen it by pulling down one of the abutments and putting girders up. With regard to the preamble of the bill generally, is it true ? Yes. It will be a great public benefit, but at the same time I acknowledge that it will be an improvement to the traffic of the Ship Canal. Cross-examined by lr. ,Pembroke Stephens: I admit that there has been no disposition to throw unnecessary difficulties in the way of the Ship Canal en the part of the Warrington Corporation.. On the contrary, they have been strong supporters of the scheme. Although these roads are not in the municipal boundary they come very closely upon it, and lam aware that there is a measure before Parliament, for the extension of the boundaries of the borough.

You he put one swing bridge, and you now propose to put one high level bridge for the con- venience of the North-Western station, :and on the main road to Warrington? Yes. Having reduced the communications to two, it becomes all the more necessary that those com- munications should be substantial ones, does it not? Limiting the observation to a certain extent,' agree with you. Taking the substituted swing bridge, we will adopt that, but as to the high level bridge, thaS must in the first place be sufficientlyhigh ? Yes— about 77 feet clear of the water level.
--T- hat- Will involve considerably steep gradients? Yes, the canal is in a deep cutting there, but so far
as tkle bridge is concerned, it wotild be 45 to 50 feet above the ground level.

Don't you think where you have roads at a steep gradient approaching a bridge that they should have all the width that your powers enable you to give them? I acknowledge that when taking up a steep gradient it is better to have a wide road. And now I understand you are willing to increase the width of the roads on each side of the bridge to 36 feet of width? Yes, if we can agree on othet matters. It is not always easy to make a bridge the same width as a road, but it would not be a very great expense, and I think it would modify matters very much. Mr. Balfour Browne: I think that after what Mr. Williams has said, seeing that the road is conceded, and that he can without very great eipense make the bridge the width that is desired. I think (ui the whole that the ship Canal Company ought to make that concession, especially as Mr. Williams does not seem to have any serious ebjection. We shall now only have to settle the terms of the clauses, so that I think that is all we want to trouble yout lordships with.
Mr. Pembroke Stephens: You will save your old conditions as to gas and sewer pipes? Mr. Balfour Browne: Yo.s, certainly.
Subsequently clauses carrying out— the arrange: ment referred to were submitted to the Committee, and the opposition was withdrawn and the pre— amble declared passed.
WARRINGTON:
NATIONAL PROVINCIAL BANK Or ENGLAND.
_ A branch of the National Provincial Bank of England was opened in Warrington on Monday. The premises are situated in Bridge-st., and the manager in charge is Mr. J. W. Beevers.

div.head: FALL FROM A SWING IN THE PARR.
div.p: FALL FROM A SWING IN THE PARR.

A lad named Alfred Clough, whose parents live in Orford-st.,was playing on the swings in the park on Saturday morning, when he let go his hold of the rope and fell, sustaining a simple fracture of the fore arm. He was taken to the Infirmary.

div.head: MUSIC IN THE RAMS.
div.p: MUSIC IN THE RAMS.

The band stand in the park was occupied for the first time this season on Monday evening, when a varied selection of music was given by St. Paul's Sunday School Band. Mr. Robert Smith was con- ductor. The weather being line there was a large attendance of the public.
