Gibson and Son, Warrington, and the re-seating has been entrusted to Messrs. R.. A. Naylor, of Warrington. Mr. William Owen, architect, of Warrington, has prepared the designs. APPLETON WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.

The.e-ch-o-o-1-;erm—o—n-sin connection with the Apple- ton Wesleyan Chapel were preached, on Sunday afternoon and evening, by the Rev. John Gunnell, superintendent of the Warrington circuit. The congregations were large, and collections were made in aid of the Sunday School, realizing the Bum of £8 10s. FLOWER SERVICE AT ST. JAMES'S CIIIIRCH.

The annual flower service was held in St. James's- Church, Latchford, on Sunday afternoon. There was a large congregation, the service being-con- ducted by the Vicar, the Rev. F. Slater. The grow- ing and cut flowers, some o; which were very choice, were sent after the service to the hospitals- of the town.

div.head: LOCAL EX.H_IBITOIt AT LEEDS.
div.p: A LOCAL EX.H_IBITOIt AT LEEDS.

Among the exhibits at the Leeds International Exhibition, now being held, are two cases of sped-- men wire from the establishment of Messrs. William Smith and Son, patent wire manufacturers, Dallam Wire Works, Warrington. One of the cases contains' guitar and mandolin wires, and the other specimens - of various kinds of musical wire.

div.head: APPLETON HALL FETE.
div.p: APPLETON HALL FETE.

The gross receipts on the two days' fete at Apple- ton amounted to nearly £4OO. From this sum must be deducted the expenses of the fete, which were necessarily rather large. The balance, it is stated will not be more than sufficient to defray the cost of what the Vicar and churchwardens consider requisite for the church and schools.

div.head: BURTONWOOD SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: BURTONWOOD SCHOOL BOARD.

At the monthly meeting of this Board on Tuesday evening there were present Messrs. James Warbur- ton, Norcott, and Fairclough. Bills which were passed for payment amounted to £72 18s. ; and school pence received during the month had been £2O ss. 3d. A vote of condolence was passed with the Rev. H. Wilson on the death of his son.

div.head: Sr. ANNE'S CHOIR.
div.p: Sr. ANNE'S CHOIR.

The junior members of this choir bad their annual - pic-nic trip to Southport; last Saturday, in charge of their organist, Mr. Percy Randall, and Mr. James Baird (choir secretary). After visiting the pier. _ winter gardens, and circus, donkey racing and boating were indulged in. A good substantial dinner and tea were provided. Warrington was reached in safety about 8.30, after a day's thorough enjoyment.
BOWLB.-WARRINGTON V. AINTREE.

The ret-tUrii—Mat.,Ch 6.e-t;We-n-ul4-;;;;;;;)-iion and Aintree clubs was played on the ground of the former at Arpley on Saturday afternoon, and after a most enjoyable game resulted in a victory for the visi- tors. At the conclusion of the match the players adjourned to the Norton Arms Hotel, Latchforil, where they sat down to an excrllent dinner, ~upp- lied by Councillor Joseph Taylor, the landlord. The chair was occupied by Mr. Thomas Morris, under whose presidency an enjoyable evening- was spent. Several toasts were proposed, and a selection of vocal music was given.

SUDDEN DEATH OF A LABOITIOUL On Monday afternoon Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, attended at the Bridwell parade-room, where he conducted an inquiry into the circum- stances of the death of a brewer's laboir.er named Samuel Massey, which occurred on Wednehday- week, at his residence, in Hall-st. From the evid- ence that was adduced it appeared that the deceased was at work at Wilderspool Brewery, on Tuesday morning, about eight o'clock,when he fell down the stairs and injured his left arm. lie was at that time carrying a bag of sugar on his back, lie did not return to his work on Wednesday, althongh he appeared to be well and cheerful. He went to bed about eleven o'clock, and shortly afterwards he s iid to his brother, who was sleeping with hiin, " I ain going home. Good bye. Meet me in Heaven." The jury returned a verdict to the effect that death was apparently due to natural causes, possibly acceler- ated by the fall.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

EMULATING A "NOBLE" EXAMPLE. On Monday morning the Warrington magistrates had :before them a young man named Thomas Baguley, who was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Dial-st. on Saturday night. It was his eighth appearance, and Inspector James, after the case had been proved, remarked that the prisoner was a son of the celebrated "Peter Baguley."—Alderman Harrison : Emulating the " noble " example of his father.—A fine of ss. including costs was inflicted. THB CATAPULT DEMON AT WORK. •

At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday morninz, a youth named Albert Saunders, living in Philip- street, off Winwick-street, appeared before the magis- trates to answer a summons charging him with throwing stones in Walker-st., on the 15th Inst. It was proved that the defendant shot a stone from a catapult, which hit a boy named France, knocking out one of his eves. The inpred boy was taken to the Manchester Infirmary and underwent an operation, the doctors stat- ing that the sight of the eye had been destroyed. The Bench imposed a fine of 305., and costs Bs. A NEGLECTFUL FATHEEL

On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, a labourer named Joseph Charnock, was charged with having neg- lected to maintain his three children, who had, in conse- quence, become chargeable to the Union. Mr. Basil Shearer said that the children were admitted to the Workhouse in March, 1889, and up to the present had cost the Guardians £4B. Theprisoner had already served two terms of imprisonment for neglecting them. He •came out of goal early in May, and had been in work since, but had not attempted to pay anything towards the children's maintenance. The Bench adjourned the case for four weeks, to give the father another opportunity of providing for his children.

div.head: DRUNK ha THE POLICE COURT.
div.p: DRUNK ha THE POLICE COURT.

At the Warrington Police Conrt, on Tuesday, two .young men named Michael Callighan and Thomas Gla- vin were brought up in custody on a charge of having been drunk and disorderly in the Police Court, on the previous morning. They were also charged with having played pitch and toss on the 15th inst., in Cloth Hall- yard. It appeared that the prisoners attended the court on Monday, to answer summonses charging them with the latter offence As the proceedings at the court were rather psolonged, they adjourned to an adjoining beer- . house, wi-h the result that when their cases were called on:they were too drunk to plead. Callighan was sent to prison for a month for playing at pitch and toss, and for the drunkenness he was fined ss. and costs, with the alternative of another seven days in jail in default of payment. Glavin was sent to prison tor a fortnight for the gambling offence, and fined Ss. and costs for the drunkenness, or seven days imprisonment. A CATALOGUE OF THEFTS.—SOME HEAVY SENTENCES. Several cases of stealing were dealt with at Warring- ton Borough Court, on Saturday. Martin Mulhall was charged with having stolen from the premises of Thomas Williams, John-st., on the 13th inst., a bag containing 331bs. of screws, value 205., and on the 19th inst., nine gate hinges value 4s. Prisoner was occasionally employed by prosecutor, and whilst taking out quantities of material for his master, pilfered the articles mentioned in the charge. When apprehended the prisoner admitted that he had stolen the goods and sold them. The Bench committed the prisoner for three months with hard abour.—The next case was that of a girl. named Sarah Ann Hadley, 12 years of age, living with her parents in John-st., who was in custody ona charge of having stolen from the dwelling-house of John Thomas Harrison, baker, Winwick-rd., on the 14th May, a sum of £2 9s. 11d., a shawl, and an apron, value ss. The sirl had been in the employ of the prosecutor as a domestic servant. On the 14th ult, she left her place and ran away from the town, taking with her the money and articles mentioned in the charge. She was found at Knutsford, and brought back to her parents by the relieving officer. The father was present in court, and asked the magistrates to send the girl to an industrial school. She had run away from home on three occasions, and had been a continual source of trouble to her parents. The Bench ordered the girl to be imprisoned for 14 days' and afterwards be sent to a reformatory for five years.—Catherine Taylor was charged with having, on the 10th May, stolen a silver watch, value £2, from Charles Cleaver; and Thomas Miskell was charged with having received the watch knowing it to have been stolen. The prisoners were before the Court four or five weeks ago, but as no owner could be found for the watch they were discharged. Miskell, however, was afterwards sent to goal for a month for assaulting Taylor. Ile had been liberated that morning, and on leaving prison was re-arrested by P.C. Monoghan on the present charge.—The prisoners were ,committed for two months with hard labour. A THEATRICAL SCANDAL. - -- •

At the Warrington Police Court, on Saturday, Marian Ashton, an actress, was charged with having been drunk and diqorderly in Horsemarket-st. on the previous even- ing. PQ. Corbett stated that at ten minutes to eleven -o'clock he found the prisoner, who was very drunk, creating a disturbance outside the Hop Pole public-house. She was using abusive language to a woman in the 'crowd. He asked the prisoner for her address, but she refused to give it. With the assistance of P.C. Barnett, he took her to the Bridewell. She was very noisy all the way. The landlord of the Hop Pole said that he had to forcibly eject the prisoner from his house. Prisoner said that while at the Hop Pole she met the woman with whom her husband was living. The woman asked her why she kept following her. Prisoner replied ‘'How dare you look me in the face, far less speak to me ?" And then under great provocation, she abused the woman. The 'Bench remarked that with the provocation they had nothing to do. They had only to look at the conduct of the prisoner. Three witnesses had proved that she was drunk, and for that offence she would have to pay a fine of ss. and costs. At a sitting of the magistrates on Monday Mr. Arthur Browne made an application to the Bench to vary an order under which Edward Arthur Ashton was directed to pay a sum of 129. a week towards the maintenance of his wife. He pointed out that since the order was made by Messrs. John White and Charle White, magistrates, the means of the wife had greatly improved; in fact, she was earning more money than her husband. Only on Saturday she concluded an engagement at the Comedy Theatre, Manchester. She had been in receipt of as much as £2 2s. a week. He asked the order to be re- duced to such a reasonable sum as would prevent the wife getting drunk so often—she was before the Court on Saturday—and creating frequent disturbances outside the theatre and her husband's lodgings. Mrs. Ashton was called and denied having received the salaries men- tion,ed. She was not paid anything in Manchester. At Widnes she obtained 2.55. a week. The Bench expressed themselves unwilling to alter an order made by other magistrates, and accordingly granted an adjournment Isotil such time as one or both of the magistrates in question should be on the bench. AMUSING CASS AT DARKSBIIIIT. •

Jeseph Cliffe, of Whitley Inferior, was summoned to the Daresbury Sessions on Tuesday, for having on the 22nd June alfowed his dog to be at large in a public place there, in contravention of the Rabies Order. Sergeant Dutton gave evidence as to seeing the dog on the foot- path near defendant's house. The defendant: It is not a public foothpath. People who use it do so on sufferance. I have in my possession the original plan of the whole estate. Serg,lint Dutton: The dog was on the public footpath. Th. Chairm in : I have known the spot for a long time. but I neverknevr there was a footpath there. Have you ever turned people back, Mr. Cliffe? Defend- ant: Many a time. Now we allow people to use the footpath, but no one has the right to do so witbout my permission. I stop people now and then. That road has cost me from £BOO to £l,OOO, and for that man (point- ing to the officer) to come and stay at my gate and watch me and my deg is a shame. If I cannot take my dog out I will slat out of the country. The Chairman (to the officer) : Unless you can give us better evidence we shall have to decide against you. I have known the place all my life. The officer: The road is used by the public. I have used it constantly. The defendant: Sadly too moth. (Laughter.) Superintendent Large to the officer) : Have you been turned back? The officer': No, sir. The defendant: No, but if he lives a bit longer I will turn him back. (Laughter.) Mr. Cliffe called the defendant in a case previously heard, and Mr. Gough, who said he had lived in Whitley Inferior 60 years. He knew the footpath in question. There was no public way across it. The Bench dismissed the case. Defendant: A dirtier or a meaner case was never brought before the magistrates. I have always tried to keep the law. as Sergeant Booth will tell you. I want to Irak Sergeant Dutton—The Clerk: The case has been dismissed. The defendant: Stop a bit. I shall not be stopped like this. You need not think you are going to I frighten me out of court. If you do you're a "rum un." (Laughter.) I want to ask the sergeant of police what he is watching my house for. The Clerk: It will do no good ;0 ask such a question. The defendant: I argue that point, and I want to know if I am to submit to being watched in my house night and morning ? The Clerk: If you have a complaint to make write to the -Chief Constable. Defendant: I will write to no one, but if he (Sergeant Dutton) comes again I will put him in the mud. (Laughter.) He must not think lam going to be frightened by a police constable. (Renewed laughter.) Good morning, gentlemen.

div.p: MINOR CASES.

including costs; John Flaherty, Bridge-st., Sunday night, fined ss. including cost.; Charles Magrath, Dial- court, 14th June, fined 53. and costs; John Dunn, Silver-1 st., 12th inst., fined 6s. 6d. including costs Mary Ann Leach, Cockhedge-lane, 12th June, discharged with a caution ; William Bailey, Peter-st., 15th inst., fined 10s. and costs ; Bridget Toole, Bridge-st., 15th inst.,fined ss. and costs; Mary Gibbons, Bridge-st., 15th inst., fined 53. and costs • and Bodelia Knockton, Winwick-st., 16th inst., discharged on promising to sign the pledge. BAD Lexemaes.--Winifred Jennings was sent to gaol for 14 days for having used bad language, on the 16th June, in Winwick-st. BROGING.—Henry Thatcher was charged with begging on Saturday evening, in Liverpool-road. He was dis- missed with a caution.

Ty:ern—Joseph Lee, a forge labourer, pleaded guilty to stealing a jug from a cart in the Market-place, be- longing to Richard Bailey. He was apprehended with thejug in his possession. The Bench ordered prisoner to pay a fine of 20s. including costs, or go to prison for seven days' hard labour. STONE-THROWING.—Henry Turner, a boy, was fined 2s. ed. and costs for throwing stones in Dial-st., on the 15th June. CHARGE AGAINST A REFRESHMENT-HOUSE KEEPER. Thomas Mayhall, St. James'-st., was summoned for hav- ing, on the 14th June, being a licensed refreshment- house keeper, allowed his premises to be open during I prohibited hours. P.C. Bell proved that the defendant's tripe shop was open, and customers served in it at 11.20 p.m. Defendant stated that the house was not licensed. The Magistrates' Clerk remarked that in that event the Bench could not convict. The case was accordingly dis- missed.

FURIOUS DitlVlNG.—James Paton, fish hawker, Wigan, was summoned for allowing his cart to stand for an un- reasonable time in Winwick-st., on the 14th inst. ; and for driving furiously in Winwick-st. on the same date. Mine of 10s. and costs was imposed. A VIOLENT DOG.—Christian Bowers, butcher, Church- st., was summoned for not keeping his dog under proper control. According to the evidence, the dog was chained in the defendant's yard near an opening by which the school children passed. As a boy, four years of age, was passing the dog dashed out and bit him in the thigh. The boy was at present under treatment for the wound at the Infirmary. An order was made that the animal be kept under control ; and for the payment of costs, 203.

Sormsv GAMING.—George Hicks, John McDonough, Thomas Gavin Michael Callggan, Edward Flanagan,' Thomas Welsh, Sauce, John Kelly, and Thomas Kelly, young men, were summoned for playing pitch and toss in Clothhall-yard, on the 15th inst. Gavin and Callaghan came into court drunk, and were remanded until Tuesday. Welsh, Sauce, and John Kelly, who were able to prove an alibi, were discharged. Flanaghan, a cripple, was lined 5s including costs ; and Wicks, Thos. Kelly, and McDonough were committed for a month with hard labour each. TIIE3DAY.—Before Mr. R Garnett and Mr. E. M. Crosfield.

A MELANCHOLY REcoen.—Edward Crosby (28) was fined 10s. and costs for having been drunk and dis- orderly in Buttermarket-st., on the previous night. VAGRANCY.—Kichard and Sarah Jane Dilley, husband and wife, were charged with sleeping out, and the latter was also charged on a warrant with having been drunk and disorderly in Dial-st., on the 24th March. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.—Several persons were dealt with for neglecting to regularly send their children to school. Mr. George Riley prosecuted on behalf of the School Attendance Committee.

WigniszsDAy.—Before Aldermen Holmes and Chandley, and Mr. John Fairclough. THEFT FRON A Curium LlNE.—Annie Dooley pleaded guilty to having stolen two aprons, value is. 6d., from a clothes line in Naylor-st., on the night previous. She was sent to prison for a month, with hard labour. DURNEENNES9.—John Johnson was charged with hav- ing been drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street on the previous afternoon, and with having assaulted Constable Griffiths. He was fined 10s. and costs.

A VIOLENT VAGRANT.—Richard Dilley was charged with sleeping out in Bostock-st., and with having assaulted Constable Jones, on the same morning. When the officer found prisoner, the latter assaulted him and resisted apprehension. He was sent to prison for a month, with hard labour. THURSDAY—Before Aldermen Chandley and Sutton.

ihiorncEtiwv.ss.—Jane Waterworth, whO was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket- st., on the day previous was discharged on promising not to offend aglin.—Ambrose Harvey, for having been drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road, on the previous day, was fined ss. and costs.—Christopher Fairbank, for having been drunk in Winwick-st., on the same morning, was fined ss. including costs....

THE EDUCATION Am—Thosnas Goulding was sum- moned for having neglected to send his child to school, and was fined 55., including costs. Mr. B. Shearer proved the case. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison.
DRUNKENNESS.—Ann Price was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Winwick-st., on the pre- vious afternoon, but was discharged.
DARESBURY PETIT SESSIONS.
T UESDAY.—Before Messrs. Edward Greenali (in the chair),
James Marson, and W. C. Jonei:

DRUNK ON LICENSED PREMISES.--Tnseph Hillidge was charged with having on the 27th May last, at Preston-o'- th'-Hill, been drunk on licensed premises kept by Mr. W. Whitlow. P.C. 238 proved the case. He said he visited the Red Lion, Preston Brook, at 9.30 p.m. on the 27th May, and in the tap•roorn he found five men, including the defendant, who was drunk. He drew Mr. Whitlow's attention to the man, and Mr. Whitlow said "Joe, you are drunk again. Come out of this. I have told you many a time."—Mr. Whitlow, who was called, stated that the defendant did not appear to be drunk, and had not his attention been called to his condition he would have served him with more beer if he had asked for it.— The defendant was fined is. and costs. Bs. 6d. DRUNKENNESS.—The following persons were fined for drunkenness :—Henry Rocks, at Appleton, on the 26th May, fined ss. and costs; Henry Taylor, 26th May, at Preston-o'-'th Hill, ss. and costs ; William Webb, at Preston-o'-thcHill, on the 28th May, 53. and costs; Jos. Brady, Bth June, at Acton Grange. ss. and costs; John Johnson, 7th June, at Grappenhall, ss. and costs; John Highfield, 23rd June, at Higher Walton, ss. and costs. STRAYING RORSRS.—Jonathan Pilling, charged with allowing a horse to stray on the highway at Appleton, on the 25th May, was fined Is. and costs.—William Whitlow was summoned for having, on the sth June, at Dutton, allowed two horses to stray on the highway, and was fined in a similar amount. _ _

UNMUZZLED Doos.—Henry Hayes, George salt, and Owen Gough, were each fined a shilling and costs for allowing their dogs to be at large on different dates.— Phillip James was charged with a similar offence at Preston-o'th'-Hill, on the 31st March, and was fined a shilling and costs; John Miller, charged with a similar offence at Stretton, on the 7th June, was also fined in the same amount. REMOVING CATI'LE WITHOUT LICENSES.—Edwin Richard- son, grocer, Paddington, was summoned for having on the 9th inst., caused a cow to be moved from Poulton to Appleton without a license. Joseph Whitfield, labourer, was summoned for moving the animal. Mr. Richard- son said he only kept one cow, and had he been aware of the order, for his own sake he would not have had it moved. It had never been on the road before since it came into his possession. It was being taken to Apple- ton Hall Farm. Mr. Richardson was fined ss. and costs; the case against Whitfield was dismissed. —James Marsh and Joseph Marsh, a lad, were charged with a similar offence. The boy was discharged, and the elder defend- ant was fined is. and costs. _ _

ing Jessie Mary Rutter. aged 8 year", daughter of P.C. Rutter of Albert Terrace.—The prisoner was§ committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIOSIB.. Monnev.—Before Mr. Chas. Reynolds and Mr Jas. Handley. It was alleged that both boys were unmercifully beating the animal Wren sticks. Harding, who was in charge,said the donkey wasstupid. He was fined 6d. and costs. Roberts, who is a very young boy, was dismissed on the ground that ke was acting under the instructions of Harding. DRUNKENNESS. Mottram, Joseph Whalley, John Ratcliffe, Wm. Green, Arthur Beckett, and Wm. Blower, boys, were dealt with in a like manner for calming an obstruction in Green- way-rd. HE WENT Ronunr.r.—Toseph Rowlands was charged with having been drunk whilst in charge of a horse in Regent-st., on Saturday night, and also with assaulting P.C. Benfield.—Sergeant Goslind said that on Saturday night, about eight o'clock, he saw the prisoner who was drunk, go into a public-house in Regent-st. When he came out he went to his pony, which was standing at the door, and as he attempted to get on to it, but was incapable of riding it owing to his condition, he was ordered to go home. He declined to do so, and after setting the police at defiance for some time,. P. C. Ben- field caught hold of him to bring him to the police sta- tion. After taking him some distance down the street, prisoner asked " Are you going to take me to the police station ?" And on receiving a reply in the affirmative he said "I shall go roughly." He then commenced to kick, but was thrown down, and the handcuffs• placed on him.—P. C. Benfield said the prisoner kicked him I three times on the legs whilst he was on theground.— The Chairman said he found that the prisoner had been fined and been sent to prison 27 times since 187ffi He however, had not been before the Court for size months, and as the assault was not a serious one,.prisoner woirld be ordered to pay 20s. and 13s. 4d. costs for the two offences.

No FED:mous INTENT. —Joseph Hughes,.vras charged with having stolen a pair of boots value ss. the property of Robert Tagg. Tagg missed the boots fromthe kitchen of the Welsh Harp beerhouse, Cooper-st.,, on the 2.0t1t inst., and subsequently he found the prisoner was wear- ing them. The prisoner contended they were his, but the prosecutor proved they were his by certain, mark& upon them. As the prisoner had left his own shoes at the Welsh Harp the Bench considered that there was no. proof of felonious intent, and discharged the prisoner'

EQUAL TO TIM Occamorf.,—Ellen Blythe was summoned for assaulting James Ainsworth, on the 3rd inst., and a cross-summons was taken out by Blythe against Ains- worth. Mr. Chnrton represented Blythe.—James Ains- worth, of Newtown, Frodshats, said that the assault on him consisted of being struck several times about the head.--Mr. Trafford (magistrate's clerk) She boxed your ears I suppose f—Complainant : She did that. (Laughter.)—Mr. aturton, for the defence,. said that Ainsworth nearly ran over his client's daughter, and damaged the hoop ased for carrying water. Nog wonder that when she met him she gave him a bit of her mind. He had a whip in his hand, and struck her with it, whereupon she returned the blows in self-defence.. Wit- nesses were called, but before they had all been exarnined the Bencli'said they had heard enough of the case, and dismissed both summonses.

Torrarrirv. Aannevee.---Joseph Tollett, of Frodgitem, answered a summons taken out by Elizabeth kndrews charging hub with assaulting: her on the 4th inst. Dir. Churton appeared for complainant, who, he said, was a respectabledady. and the daughter of a gentleman who owned son/eland adjacent to the defendant's house. For a long time past the Andrews had been annoyed by the children of 'Fblletts throwing stones, as they passed along;. 4 a private lane belonging to them,. and leading to their- i Ihnd. On the date natned'NlievAndrows received informa— tion that the cows were being run after, and late at night she went to the field,. and in the lane she met defendant's son. She toldliimbe•had no right there, and warned him off: Declisingto,obey, sbe took hold of him for the purpose •of ejecting hinb„ when the defendant came, struck her on the wrist, and released the lad. She did not wish to press the case, her only wish being to show the party that they' had no right to trespass on the land.—The Bench therefore-dismissed the case en pay- ment of costs.

DRUNBENNESS.—For this offence a fine of si: and cots was imposed upon each of the following :—Mary Porter;. Gerrard-st. ; Richard Nash, Major Cross-st. ;, Thomas Humphreys, Wareing-st. ; Patrick Kelly, no residence;;, Cornelius McGarra, Railway-st. ; and Owen Smith: A MBILSEY-RAAD Row.—William Keenaghan,. a. big fellow, of no fixed abode, was charged, under a warrant, with creating a breach of the peace on Tuesdaf, the 27th ult. About half-past five o'clock P.C. Daviesen saw the prisoner fighting with Mr. Herrirnan, the landlord ofthe Mersey Hotel, and also five or six others engaged in a. similar manner, and who had assaulted Mr. Herriman. There was a large crowd of people present. Mr. Lewin, said Mr. Elerriman had been laid up in consequence ofrl the assaults, but he could not find out who his assailants were, or he would have summoned them. The prisoner was bound over to keep the peace for three montus, or go to gaol 14 days.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. Taunsmax.—Before Mr. H. Wade Deacon and Mr. 11.. Gaskell, A Row AT "Du. GERRARD'S. —Thomas Gerrard, land- lord of the Alexandra Hotel, Victoria-rd., and William Fildes (alias Downer), of Little John-st., were summoned for having caused a breach of the peace, by fighting in Victoria-rd., on the 19th inst. On the application of the solicitor for Gerrard, the case against him was adjourned for a week. Fildes was called and pleaded guilty, under great provocation.—P.S. Clarkson said that :bout a quarter to nine on the night in question a large crowd was assembled in Victoria-rd., forming a circle round the defendants who were fighting. They struck at each other in a savage manner. With the assistance cf P.S.'s McGregor and Laing, witness separated the defendants. They were not stripped.--P.S. McGregor said he saw Gerrard and a man named Joseph Harrison put Fildes out of the Alexandra Hotel in a savage manner and then Gerrard strucleFfldes on the face. He never saw Fades strike Gerrard.—P.S. Laing corroborated.—Mr. Deacon, said on this evidence, they should dismiss the case against Fildes. The case against Gerrard would be heard in a. week.

Tyr.—Francis Ryan, 43 Pitt-st., pleaded guilty to having stolen a pair of boots valued at 2s. 6d., the prom petty of a youth, named John McQuade, of 12.Crom, well-st. While playing on the waste ground near West Bank Dock, McQuade took off his boots, and while he was away the prisoner took them and pawned them for. is. 6d. at Imison's. The prisoner was ordered to receive four strokes with the birch rod.

DRIMBNNESS.-A fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon each of the following :—Catherine Hynes, Marsh-st. ; Mary Jane Riley, Nelson-st. ; John Higgins, Bedford-st. ;. Timothy Riordan, Dock-st. : Thomas Tausey, Gerrard- st. ; Ann Bryan, Poole-st. ; Martin Grady, North,st. ; Wm. Wallace, Windermere-st. ; Henry Waters, Fara- worth-st. ; and Jane Parry, Wright-st. BREACHRS ov THR F BACH. —John Willis, Davies-at.,,and Elizabeth Jones, Nelson-st., were each bound over, to keep the peace for two months for creating disturbance in the street.

Ping AND Toss.—James Rourke and Thomas Cleary, youths of Aiforde-st., were summoned for playing pitch and toss in Alforde-st., on the 15th June, and a fine of is. and costs 7s. 6d. was imposed upon each de- fendant. _ _

div.head: OPENING THE NEW WIMBLEDON.
div.p: OPENING THE NEW WIMBLEDON.

The Princess of Wales will formally open the new Wimbledon either on Saturday,. the 12th, or Monday, the 14th July. The ceremony, it is understood, will be similar to that which took place thirty-one years ago, when the Wimbledon ranges were opened by the Queen firing the first shot. The arrangements for the camp are well advanced, and are confidently expected to be com- pleted some days before the opening. •
DEATH OF LORD STAMFORD.

News has been received of the death of the Earl of Stamford. who was in his 78th year, at Wynberg, Cape of Good Hope. The deceased (the Rev. Harry Grey) was the eighth Earl, and was in holy orders of the Church of England. He was thrice married, the last occasion being in December, 1880, and he has left a daughter, who was born in 1881, the only issue of his marriages. He will be succeeded in the title by his nephew William, who was born in 1850, and who was formerly professor of classics andphilosophy at Codring- ton College, Barbadoes.

div.head: SAN SALVADOR.
div.p: SAN SALVADOR.

"SUDDEN DEATH" OF THE PRESIDENT. New YORK, MONDAY.—A despatch from San Salvador announces that General Menendez, the President, died suddenly last night at the conclusion of a banquet given on the occasion of the fifth anniversary of his entry into San Salvador and the defeat of the Zaldivar faction. During the panic which was occasioned by the President's sudden death General Marcia and a few others were killed at the barracks. General Carlos Czeta' the leader of the forces, is now incommand, and up to the present tranquility prevails.

div.head: FIVE LIVES LOST IN THE ENGLISH
div.p: FIVE LIVES LOST IN THE ENGLISH
CHANNEL.

A fatal collision occurred in the English Channel on Tuesday afternoon, about 20 miles south-west of Port- land, between the screw steamer Umbile, bound from Natal to London, with a general cargo, and the barque Ethel, Captain Alfred Percy Ross, bound to Brisbane, when one of the crew of the steamer and four of the barque were killed by falling spars. The Ethel, whose crew numbered 16, sank about three minutes after the collision. The survivors including Mr. Stobart (one of the owners), with his wife, two children, and his sister- in-law' were conveyed by the steamer Umbile to Portlead, where they were transferred to the ss.Tremer, and taken to Weymouth.
SUPPOSED MURDER OF A BROTHER

_ An Airdrie telegram states that early on Sunday morn- ing the dead body of a young man, named -James M'Gowant was found at the foot of a steep embankment between Mossend Railway Station and Holytown. De- ceased, with his father, brother, and several friends, had attended the fair at Holvtown on Saturday, and when the party rehire-anal were the worse for drink. De- ceased and his brother Peter quarrelled during the even- ing. Blows were struck, but the two were separated, and one of the men went towards home, while the other remained stationary. The first brother left the party to have it out with his brother James, and nothing more was seen of either until James' body was found. Peter M'Gowan has been arrested.
THE NEWFOUNDLAND FISHERIES DIS-
ATTE,---SpW)ITS COLLISION.

According to intelligence from St. George's nay, pub- lished by the " New York Herald," a conflict recently occurred in a cove at Port-au-Port, on the south-west portion of the French shore, between some two hundred Newfoundlandm and Frenchmen, the crews -of fishing boats. The quarrel arose out of the question of the pos- session of choice positions for catching bait. The Frenchmen were at first successful, but were eventually driven off. No firearms or knives were used, the comba- tants fighting with clubs, oars, boathooks, &c. No fatal injuries were inflicted on either side, but bones were broken in a number of cases. The Frenchmen were in the minority, and therefore suffered the most.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY DIVORCE CASE.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY DIVORCE CASE.

In the Divorce Division on Saturday. before Sir James Hannen, Mrs. Evelyn Isabel Bethune, a lady of consider- able fortune, residing in London sought a dissolution of marriage on the ground of the adultery and cruelty of her husband, Mr. Charles C. Bethune. According to the evidence of the petitioner, whose maiden name was Goldsmid, she married the respondent in February, 1886. Her husband was entitled to a small estate in Scotland, which was heavily mortgaged. Petitioner had property which brought her in bet Ween £3,000 and £4,000 a year, and on her marriage she paid off the debts of her hus- band, which amounted to £4,000, and made a settlement of £l,OOO a year on respondent, to take effect after her death. Respondent had refused to consummate the mar- riape, and would not occupy the same room as his wife. He had also struck her, and said he loathed and hated her—Two witnesses were called to prove that the res- pondent had committed adultery with A Madame Demar, whom' he had visited at Maida Vale.—No defence was offered, and his lordship pronounced a decree nisi for the dissolution of the marriage, with costs.

div.head: A. TEBRIBLE IRAGEDY IN RUSSIA.
div.p: A. TEBRIBLE IRAGEDY IN RUSSIA.

News has reached St. Petersburg by mails from Odessa of a family tragedy lately enacted in the village of Warowka, a suburb of that place. A son of a farmer named Kowalenko married the young Countess Helene Laskowski, against the will of his father. He brought his young wife to the farmer's homestead, where ske was asked to help in the household and field labours. The young gentlewoman was unable to comply with this , request, and the father-in-law thereupon illtreated his I son on account of the arist3cratic demeanour of his bride, until finally the young people quitted the house and went to live with Count Laskowski. Old Bowalenko, who lost a valuable workman by the departure of his son, secured the latter's arrest by the village trustee on the plea that he had'evaded parental authority. The young man was kept imprisoned on bread and water for five days, and then underwent a flogging with the knout. He was sent back to his father's house in an utterly exhausted condition, and immediately after his arrival he committed suicide by poisoning himself.

div.head: ANGLO-GERMAN AGREEMENT.
div.p: THE ANGLO-GERMAN AGREEMENT.

A Heligoland telegram says the formal cession of Heligoland to Germany will, it is expected, take place in October next, when Prince Henry of Prussia, the Emperor's brother, will come with a German squadron to take over the island from the representatives of her Britannic Majesty. The island is not to be placed under the rule of the Governor of the Elbe Duchies, nor to form part of the Prussian province of Schleswig-Holstein, but like the Reichsland Alsace-Lorraine, it will be admin- istered directly by the Imperial Government, with the rights of a separate State of the German Empire.

OPINION OF THE ISLANDERS. The" Pall Mall Gazette" publishes the following cable message.forwarded from Heligoland by its special repre- sentative who was sent there last week with instructions to ascertain the opinions of the islanders on their transfer to Germany :—" I found• the islanders greatly puzzled at the unexpected cession of their island to Germany. So far as they have taken in what it all means, I Mid them extremely hostile to the cession, and they do not conceal their indignation." FRENCH MINISTERIAL DECLARATION. In the Chamber of Deputies on Saturday, M. Deloncle put the question of which he had given notice regarding the effect of the Anglo-French Declaration of 1882, guaranteeing the independance of Zanzibar, upon the provision in the Anglo-German agreement for a British Protectorate over the Sultanate. M. Ribot, Minister of Foreign Affairs, in reply, said that Article 34 of the Berlin Convention rendered it obligatory uptin every nation desirous of establishing a Protectorate in Africa to com- municate its intentions to the other powers. Great Britain would not fail to fulfil its obligation, all the more inasmuch as in 1.883 she signed a convention engaging to respect the independence of Zanzibar. She could not, therefore, take any action without a previous under- standing with France. The reply was received with applause, and , after M. Deloncle had expressed his thanks to M. Ribot for his explanation, the House ad- journed. Both in French and German Pailiaments on Tuesday discussion of the Anglo-German agreement was post- poned at the request of the .lovernment. div.head: HELIGOLAND.
div.p: HELIGOLAND.

An authority on Naval matters, who is believed to be Rear-Admiral Werner, writing in the " Rheinische Courier," states that the possession of Heligoland is no advantage to Getmany from a practical or political point of view, but would, on the contrary, involve a large expenditure of money and be a fruitful source of anxiety. As for the island commanding the North Sea and Baltic Canal, the writer declares that the idea can- not be entertained A Berlin correspondent says that Prince Bismarck has criticised unfavourably the Angio-German agreement respecting East Africa. He considers the English pro- tectorate over Zanzibar disadvantageous to Germany.

div.p: Zattrs to tbt attar.

THE ENDOWMENT OF THE BEER BARREL. Sir,—A majority of four, good men and true, have decided that the trade whose effects are poverty, crime, and disease, is to have an advantage in spreading those three foes to humanity—an advantage no honest, useful business, ever asked for or expected, for the simple reason that no such advantage could or would be granted. But beer is to be endowed and whiskey is to be superannuated. Bravo Goschen! devout votary of Bacchus ! One would suppose from his conduct that the right hon. gentlemen has beer on the brain, and is being deluded by spirits of the still. Remedial legislation for Ireland is to be shunted in favour of beer, foreign wines, spirituous liquors, and tobacco. The Tithes Bill is to be passed (if possible). Yes, take "care of the Church ; Tory Governments are very tender towards the Church and the public-house. Don't touch them with unholy hands. They contain their supporters, and, especially before elections, they must be nursed and well cared for. The Irish Land Bill must wait for these measures to be passed ; not that the Land Bill would benefit Ireland generally, but only a small class com- pared with the bulk of the population. The impecunious landlord and the poor tenant will not be benefitted. It is the dukes, the marquises, and the earls, the rich and the wealthy absentees,who draw money from Ireland and spend it elsewhere who will be benefitted, along with the wealthy graziers and rich cattle dealers. These are the people who have benefitted by the Ashbourne Act and who will benefit by Balfour's Act, if it is ever passed. One thing seems pretty certain that before either the " Goschen Drink Endowment Bill," the" Tithes Bill," or the " Balfour Irish Landlord Relief Bill," can become law the mechanical majority must be regalvanised, and the deserters from the army of ninety must be captured and placed in the ranks again. Goschen is in trouble,Ritchie is in despair, and Balfour has the sulks. The Ministry and their supporters are in a bad way, and need to go to the country for fresh air and rest. That no doubt will be the prescription which the country doctor will insist upon. Their allies look upon their disorder with con- tempt, and they receive scant pity ftom their friends who consider that they have over-gorged themselves with Land Purchase, Tithes, Local Taxation, Heligoland, and Beer. It is more than the constitutional stomach can bear, and nothing but a period of rest and solitude can re- store them to anything like political life. May they soon obtain it !—I am, sir, yours respectfully, Sankey Bridges, June 23, 1890.
CYI4IRO.

div.head: WALKING DAY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: WALKING DAY AT WAR- RINGTON.

The Walking Day of this year was, in the point of weather, a decided contrast to that of last year. Last year there was not a drop of rain, nor even a threatening cloud, to mar the pleasures of the day, but on this occasion all the carefully made arrange- ments of the conductors of Sunday Schools were dis- turbed by adverse climatic influences. The morn- ing opened in a promising manner, their being a fine bright sunshine, but it was soon seen that these appearances were delusive, and by the time the main procession had gathered in the Park, the rain began to fall rather heavily, and though there were occasional intervals of sunshine the showers were frequent and heavy till the latter part of the after- noon, when the weather became more settled and the sun shone out pleasantly The arrange- ments made in connection with the different Sunday Schools were very similar to those of former years. The children attending the different Church Schools gathered at their various schoolrooms, and, after forming into processions, proceeded thence to the Park in front of the Town Hall: A combined procession was here formed, and the Park was left in the following order : Blue Coat School, Workhouse Schools, Parish Church and Missions Schools, St. Ann's. St. Peter's, St. Barnabas, St. Paul's and Mission, Holy Trinity -d St. James'. Following these from the Park a.... vrerd t schools schools of the Emmanuel Church, Ragged School, Salrat.Z9n Army, Legh-st. Primi- tive Methodists, and Latchford Primitive Metho- dists. After perambulatina some 0€ the prin- -aipal streets, all the scholars connected with thQ Parish Church Schools and those of Crossley-st., and Bank-st. Missions, together with the contingents from the Blue Coat, the Union Schools, and others, attended a short service at the Parish Church. There were also suitable services at the churches of St. Paul's and St. James', Latchford. The Nonconfor- mists had no combined procession,each school having an independent programme to fulfil. Some of these schools,as will be seen from the details given below, left the town by train in the course of the morning. As in other years the Roman Catholics of St. Mary's, Buttermarket-st., St. Albans, and St. Mary's, Latch- ford,fornied a separate and by no means an insigni- ficant procession with bands and banners of their own. The number of spectators who lined the streets to witness the processions was much less than in some former years and at no point except at Market-gate was there any great crush. This falling off was undoubedtly mostly due to the rain, but in addition to this, as the day was ob- served as a general holiday in the town, many of the adult population had taken advantage of the opportunity to make excursions by road or rail. Below we give details as to the manner in which the various schools were to spend the day, but it should be premised that in some cases the unfivour able weather would lead to changes in the pro- gramme.

BLUE COAT.—Number on Scholars on books 30 boys, 27 girls ; average attendance 30 boys, 27 girls ; number of teachers 3 mate; number of books in library 350; superintendents, Mr. and Mrs. Rose. As usual the Blue Coat scholars took part in the procession and attended the service at the Parish Church. They were headed by the school band. WORKHOUSE ScHoot.--Number of scholars on books, 10; number of teachers, 1 ; minister, Rev. S. Wilkinson; master, Mr. C. H. Ward. As usual these children spent the day with the scholars of Padgate Industrial School.

INDUSTRIAL SCHOOL, PAM:M.TH.—Number of scholars OR books 91 boys, 65 girls; number of teachers 2 male, 1 female ; number of books in library 165 •, Rev. S. Wilkin- son, chaplain ; superintendents, Mr. 11. M. Mines aid Mrs. Mines. The children went by the 8.30 train to Warrington, and joined the procession in the Park. After attending church they were served with buns and milk, and then walked home to Padgate. The afternoon was spent in a field at Woolston, kindly lent for the occasion by Mr. Joseph Houghton. Various games and sports were indulged in, and tea, sandwiches, buns, oranges, and nuts were provided. Messrs. Eddowes and Co. gave the children a quantity of ginger beer and cider. The school band was in attendance.

LADIES SCHOOL OF INDUSTRY.—No, of scholars on books, 169, no. of teachers, 5 female ; ministers, Rev. F. W. Willis and Rev. D. S. Hodgson. The scholars joined the church procession and took part in the service at the Parish Church. They then went to St. Elphin's Park, and joined in games with the other children there. Tea was served during the afternoon in the schoolroom.

ORFORD BerinAcks.—Number of scholars on books, 36 ' boys, 48 girls ; number of teachers, 4 male, 3 female; superintendent, Lieut. Longfield. These children after being in the procession were to spend the afternoon at St. Elphin's Park.

l'entsix Clintca.—Boys School Number of scholars on books 360 ; average attendance 270 ; number of teachers 14 male, seven female ; number of books in library 550 • I superintendents, Messrs. James Scotson and Samuel Davies.—Girls School: Number of scholars on books, 325 ; number of teachers, 24 ; superintendent, Miss Shaw.—Crossley-st. Mission School : Number of scholars on book, 128 boys, 194 .girls ; number of teachers, four male, 15 female : superintendent, Rev. C. E. Jackson.— Bank-st. Mission School : Number of scholars on books, 00 boys, 110 girls : number of teachers, 15 female ; super- intendent, Rev. D. S. Hodgson. The arrangements wit.h regard to these schools were similar to those last year. The children, having assembled at their different schools proceeded to the park, where they joined in the pro- cession to the Parish Church. The afternoon was to be spent in St. Elphin's Park, and tea was to be partaken t at the different schoolrooms. The band of the Liver- pool regiment was in attendance.

HOLY TRINITT.—Number of scholars on books, 101 boys, 169 girls, number of teachers, s.male, 16 female ; number of books in library, 300. The scholars were taken to Overton Hills, Frodsham, and they were accompanied by the Walton band. Ministers : Rev. E. C. E. Carleton B.A. Vicar, Rev. W. E. Glenn, curate, and Mr. H. G. Johnstone., superintendent. These scholars were accom:
panted by those of St. Mary's Mission, sank Quay, and Factory Yard school.

ST. BARNABAS.—Number of scholars on books, 130 boys, 120 girls ; number of teachers 6 male, 6 female; superintendent, Mr. R. Y. Woollacott ; minister, Rev. G. Al!ton. Fletcher's band headed this contingent. The
elder scholars were to proceed to Frodsham for the day, and the infants were provided with tea, &c., in the
schoolroom.
ST. ANN'S.—Number of scholars on books 150 boys
200 girls ; number of teachers, six male, eight female number of books in library, 300 • minister, Rev. T. G.
Richards, BA. ; superintendent, Mr. Edward Gibbon. The scholars of this school had tea in the afternoon at _ _
the schools, .and afterwards were taken to _Longford

OPPOSITION TO WARRINGTON EXTEN- SION SCHEME. A special meeting of Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse yester- day for the purpose of considering the proposed extension of the borough of Warrington. Mr. Knowles presided, and there were present Messrs. Hewitt, John Whitlow, H. Linaker (clerk), H. J. Linaker (deputy clerk), and J. Farrington (inspector). The Clerk said he had written to the Clerk of the Warrington Corporation for a copy of the Bill for the Extension of Warring- ton,and also a lithographed plan of the proposed extension, and his request had been complied with. In the Bill he did not find any mention of the Sani- tary Authority. Nor had the Corporation given any notice as to their proposal to include a part of the town- ship of Appleton in their scheme. The present rateable value of the tlwnship of Appleton was £13,700 and the rateable value of the portion proposed to be included in the borough of Warrington was about £2.000. There was a present debt for sewerage of £1,420 Bs. 4d., on which the interest was £54 10s. per annum and the annual repayment of principal £69 Os. Od. The amount of the debt paid off was £654 lie. Bd. Of this sewer the Corporation propose to take over about 2,050 yards, and also the main sewer outfall. The rate- able value which the Corporation intended to take over included houses and other buildings paying full sewer rate. The area proposed to be included in the borough was that part of Appleton lying on the north side of the Ship Canal, and that portion of Walton from the north , side of the Ship Canal as far as the proposed new road from the Stag Inn to Warrington. The length of dis- trict highways in the township was 15 mites and 140 yards, and the length which would be included in the extension was only a quarter of a mile, but the Corpora- tion proposed to absorb a rateable value of £2,000, and there would therefore only be left a rateable value of £11,700 tobe called upon for the repair of the remaining 141 miles of highway--On the proposition of Mr. Hewitt, seconded by Mr. Whitlow, the Clerk was in- structed to ascertain the stage at which the Bill had arrived in Parliament, and also the last day for lodging a petition against the Bill and report to the meeting on Tuesday next.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, eTTNE 28, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, eTTNE 28, 1890.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN,

The Northwicli bivislon Conservative Association and what is styled the Liberal Unionist Association for Cheshire, have severally attempted to induce some gentleman to come forward and oppose Mr. Brunner at the next election. The two associations are now joining their forces in the search for some local gentleman, who will have the hardihood to lead the forlorn hope, and it is said that "probably a selection will be made of one whose interests are bound up with the staple industry of the constitu- ency," by wnicb, of course, is meant salt. Efforts have previously been made to induce Mr. Joseph Verdin to enter the breach, but he resolutely declined; can our friend Mr. Ward now be the man?

The Runcorn Volunteer Band deserve the heartiest thanks of the community for voluntarily coming for- ward to discourse good music in the several squares of the town, and it is pleasing to notice that they have been encouraged in their" labour of lore "by large audiences. It is to be hoped the band will con- tinue their good work throughout the summer months.

Ditton Railway Bridge appears likely to cause much litigation between the Childwall Highway Board and the London and North-Western Railway , Company. The bridge was constructed by the com- pany in 1871, for the purpose of diverting the old highway and, at the same time, abolishing one of those unmitigated nuisances and dangers of a level crossing. Until the past few years the railway company have repaired the bridge,. and the road and its approaches, hut now they decline to do this work and contend that they are not liable. On the other hand the Highway Board maintain that the company are compelled to do the wnrk by Act of Parliament and whilst the dispute is proceeding tire road is neglected and is now in a dilapidated and dangerous condition. In order to enforce their view of the case, the Highway Board summoned the company before the Woolton magistrates, who after spending a day i listening to the evidence and the arguments of counsel, adjourned the ease until , Monday next. It is considered highly probable that a higher court will have to settle the dispute which is of great importance to the ratepayers of the locality. The inhabitants of Walmsley-street. Widnes, appear to consider the Murphy's undesirable as neighbours and they have a method of showing their dislike, which if not altogether unive„ismost unpleasant to those immediately concerned,. In a ease at the police court a few weeks- ago, Mrs. Murphy gave evidence which did not meet with the approval of those amongst whom her lot iseast, and it was apparently determined to drive thn Murphy family out of the locality. In their walks abroad they are threatened, and, daring to bring two of- fenders before the magistrates.the whole street is- up in arms. On Sunday morning when they shouldeave either been occupied in their religious devotion, or preparing the mid-day meal, scores- of women and chilGren besieged Murphy's resideuce and smashed nearly every pane of glass in. the house, besides breaking the window frames. The scene was described as a riot, and the .neighbourhood has been in such a ferment that it has been the special beat of a couple of constables. Three of the principal offenders were, on Thursday,sent to goat for a month in default of paying a fine. This may have a sant- tory effect, but it is by no means certain, as two other offenders, on arriving home from prison were welcomed as heroes. And this is the age of School Boards and refining influgnces The inquiry into the administratian of the police force in Runcorn resumes operations to-day at Chester Castle, and will be continued day by day until it is concluded. So far as the investigation has proceeded, the deposed Inspector O'Donnell has made some set ious charges against the general mora- lity of the town, with which a considerable propor- tion of the respectable part of the community do not agree, and,with a commendable desire to uphold the good character of the ancient port, steps are be- ing taken to draw up a petition to the Chairman of the Board of Commissioners asking him to call a public meeting of ratepayers on the question, and if necessary, passing resolutions of protest. The devil is not as black as he is painted, so we are told, and bad as Runcorn may be, it is felt by very many that the colour has been laid ,it "too thick.'
The death is announced of Mr. Charles Crompton, Q.C., formerly M.P. for the Leek Division of Stafford- shire.

div.head: TITE VOLUN I'EERS UNI)ER. CANVAS.
div.p: TITE VOLUN I'EERS UNI)ER. CANVAS.
(FROM AN "EMA.MINER." BRPORTIIR.) BLACKPOOL, FRIDAY. At Blackpool to-day the weather is but indifferent,
but on the whole the Warrington Volunteers, who have been in camp here since last. Saturday, have had fairly good atmospherical conditions, and have

managed-tO enjoy them- selves pretty well, although, as a matter of course, they have had a good deal of hard work to do when under canvas. They left Warrington on the afternoon of Saturday last, when they paraded at the Drill Hall, and thence marched to Bank Quay Railway Station, via Legh-st. and ' Sankey-et. With uniform and accoutiements all trim, they had a most soldierly appearance, and their departure was witnessed by a crowd of towns- folk. The band walked at the head of the battalion, and the muster numbered about 220 rank and file. A special train carried them to the Lancashire watering place, where some of them have since become considerably bronzed. Colonel Green- all is in command of the men, and the officers who are with the corps in camp are Lieut, Colonel ' Bolton, Captains Bridge, Widdowes, H. F. Gooch, J. D. Buckton, P. W. Baynes, and W. ilogarth, Lieutenants J. T. Smith. J. A. Edleston, F. M. Apple- ton, R. J. Chorley, and Fairclough, Quartermaster T. Hutchinson, Surgeon J. Adams, and Adjutant F. A. Adani. The Newton members of the corps joined the main body at the Newton-le-Willows station, and were under the command of Captain Widdowes. During the week men who were unable to parade on Saturday have joined the camp in driblets, and this morning there were quite a mumber who tra- velled by the six o'clock train from Bank Quay, in order to be ready for the annual inspection which, at the time of writing, has just been brought to a successful termination. The men who have come in; by the train mentioned say that rain fell heavily when they were at Wigan, but afterwards the weather to some extent improved. When the battalion arrived in camp on Saturday afternoon, or, more correctly speaking, Saturday evening, they had their work cut out. Of course, the camp had been prepared for them by the advance section, but notwithstanding that there is a great deal to do when our citizen soldiers find themselves located in tents on the shore of the deep, deep sea. Arms have to be brightened and made secure, uniforms have to be brushed and made tidy, and, above all, the volunteer has to try and make himself comfortable in unaccustomed quarters. Where there's a will there's a way, however, and by Sunday morning the camp was ship-shape, and, as the saying goes, in apple-pie order. The Rector of Warrington, the Rev. F. W. Willis, is the chaplain of the corps, and the custom being that the chap- lain shall hold service in camp, he preached an elo- quent sermon to the men on Sunday, the ordinary strength of the battalion being supplemented by some two or three hundred visitors.

For his text Mr. Willis selected the words—" Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ. No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life, that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier. And if a man also strive for masteries, yet is he IVA crowned except he strive lawfully. The husbandman that laboureth must be first partaker of the fruits " I! Timothy ii. 3-7. During his discourse Mr. Willis said that some people appeared to be under the im- pression that it was not a hard thing to spend a week during the summer at the seaside as a volun- teer, but it should be remembered that the English climate was a very treacherous one, and rain might fall throughout the week. Under those circum- stances, the men would have to rough it in their tents. Lie understood that although a volunteer got mainte- nance from the Government for the week he was in camp he received nothing for the support of his wife and children, and that was, he considered, a hardship to a workingman. Speaking of the lite of a soldier reminded him of the great Duke of Wel- lington, who, after a life of hardship, always slept in a little camp bed in his house. The text also said that "no man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this lite," and for this week at

1 itst the men must endeavour to forget their family cares and their ordinary business, and give their minds to the duties belonging to a soldier. A man was not made a soldier in a moment, and he had to give careful attention to his duties to make himself efficient. There was no short cut to become a soldier. Lastly let them take the figure of the husbandman, and learn to do the drudgery as well as the pleasant work. There was a third application— the spiritual side of the question. The command was laid upon them all to suffer hardness, and the Lord had said to each one of them, "Take up your cross and follow me." If they looked at the Saviour's life they saw what a life of hardship and self-denial it was. "The foxes have boles, the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man bath no where to lay his head." The Rector asked the men before him if their religion cost them anything. There were times when a man had to be brave for Christ —when, for instance, he heard bad language used. Then he must be prepared to be brave and to endure hardness, and if his religion did not cost him anything, the question was, "Is it worth very much?" They were naturally wrapped up in their business duties, but if a man did not think of the! world to come he would not be prepared for the hour ! of death. Christ had wrought out theirredemption, but they had to work out their own salvation, as! the time would come when no man could work. The inspection was timed for eleven o'clock, but ! it was noon before Colonel Twentyman rode into ! camp on his charger. Soon after ten o'clock there was a tremendous downpour of rain, which cleared the streets of Blackpool in a twinkling. It caused ! the men in camp to indulge in rather gloomy fore- bodings as to the pleasantness of the day's proceed- ings, but before eleven o'clock the rain had ceased,! and a brilliant sun added lustre to the event of the day. The camp is being held in a field near to the south shore, in vievr of the sea, and in a particularly healthy locality. When the rain had finished, and the sun had come out„the appearance of the camp was very pretty, the bell-tents spotted about here and there looking picturesque. While the battalion were awaiting the approach of the Inspecting Officer, Colonel Greenall and other officers of the corps put the men through a series of drills, pre- paratory to the manceuvres that they would have to take part in later on. A considerable number of onlookers assembled in the lane adjoining the field in which the camp was pitched, and it was a matter of general remark that the Warrington Volunteers looked very smart and very soldierly. The battalion paraded at eleven o'clock, but had to wait about an hour before the Inspecting Officer arrived. They were then kept bard at work for the space of two hours and a half„Colonel Twentyman ' watching their drill very closely. The field state showed a muster of 471, made up as follows:-17 officers. 28 sereeants, 34 bandsmen, and 357 rank and file. Teree officers, two sergeants, and II rank and file were absent on leave, and 19 rank and file were absent without. leave. The officers and non-com- missioned officers on parade were Colonel Greenall, in command, Major Bridge,, Captain Ridgway, Captain Widdowes, Captain Gooch, GT- ! rain Buckton, Captain Baines., Captain Hogarth, !Lieutenant Smith, Lieutenant Edeleten, Lieuten- ant Cliorley, Lieutenant Fairelough, Captain and Adjutant Adams, Quartermaster Hutchinson, Sur- geon-Major Lister, Surgeon Adams, Sergeant-Major Pennefley, Sergeant-Instructor Birch, Sergeant- instruct or Sullivan, Quartermaeter-Sergeant Heaton, Paymasl er-sergeant Whatmough, Sergeant-master ,(nitre, Bugler-Major Plinstone, Bandmaster Arm- strong, l'ioneer Warburton. and Orderly-room- clerk Mycock. , At the close of the inspection, during which Col. Greenall and other officers of the corps put the men through various drills,t he Inspectoing Officer briefly addressed the battalion. H& gave some advice to the guides of the companies as to their way of carrying out the duties of thaeposts they hold, and concluded by remarking that under all circum- stances the battalion had done very well during the inspection. Subsequently Colonel Twentyman visited the tents and inspected the books of the corps, which were found to be in a satisfactory condition. The camp will be broken up on Saturday, and some of the men have returned to Warrington this evening. xngee thelle n t , weekt h e k The hl iesatl being i onfgt eepboarttteldi oaus nil, and ednurei h b wet weather has only on two oecasilns interfered with the progress ot the drills Three parades have (e been held daily, so that the men have had plenty of work provided for them. After the inspection this afternoon a short athletic meeting was brought off, prizes being given for various events.
