NEWTON BUILDING SOCIETY. ANNUAL MEETING.

The 30th annual meeting ot the shareholders and members of the Newton-le-Willows, Haydoek and Golborne Building Society, was held in the Town Hall, Newton, on Monday night. There was a very largo attendance and Mr. J. Sankey, who presided was supported by Mr. W. H. Arnott, J.P., one of the trustees, Mr. H. Davies (solicitor), and Mr. J. Adams (secretary). Among others present were Messrs. J. W. Emmett, B. B. Gloves, H.- J. Long- ton,J. Farrow, J. Prescott, W. Liptrot,H. Brierley, &e.

div.head: ACCOUNTS: A LINELY SCENE..
div.p: THE ACCOUNTS: A LINELY SCENE..

The Secretary read the annual report, which stated that two of the properties in hand had been sold without loss, the sum outstanding on properties in hand had been reduced to £15,998 9s. 7d., and the net receipts from same were £716, 10s., being a return of £4 9s. 6th per cent. The amount outstanding on properties not in hand was £9,028 3s. 7d. The profits for the year were £1,058 us. 4d. Out of this it was proposed to pay a dividend of four pounds per cent, per annum, which would take £825 Os. 4d., leaving £233 Us. to be carried to the contingent account, which would increase that account to £4,134 us. 7d. This was nearly 26 per cent. lon the amount outstanding on properties in the society's h hands. The society consisted of 315 members, holding 2,069 invested shares, and 3,069 i purchased shares. I There were 228 persons who had withdrawn and left 'retention money amounting to £2,747 7s. 7d. The re- port added that Mr. B. B. Glover having resigned the I position he held as one of the trustees, Mr. W. H. Arnott C.C., had been elected to fill the vacant office, and had accepted the position. The accounts were duly signed by the auditors and secretary.—The Chairman considered the report quite satisfactory. The , managers had offered the Widnes property in something like five lots without any beneficial nsults, but by pri- vate treatythey had managed to dispose of two lots of property without any loss to the society. k Applause.) He thought the managers had taken a wise course in not selling the property at haphazard prices, and it would rest with the new board of managers to say whether they would sell at those reckless prices or not. He con- cluded by moving the adoption of the report. Mr. Far- row said before the statement of accounts was approved he wished te know whether the Special Committee ap- pointed twelve months ago had acted upon, orsubmitted the resolutions which were put to them, and the advice the general meeting gave them as to certain alterations. Would the Chairman or Sec.explain to the meeting the rea- son why the report of that committee was not produced? The Chairman said there was nothing in the report before the meeting bearing on the question of Mr. Farrow, and he asked someone to second the report.—Mr. B. B. Glover said the minutes of the last annual meeting ought to have been read to the meeting that night, because in those minutes it stated that a Committee was appointed to do certain work.—Mr. Arnott (interrupting) said he must support the Chairman; the question before the meeting was the passing of the report, and Mr. Glover knew very well that he was out of order in supporting Mr. Farrow. —Mr. J. W. Emmett: I just wish to say a few words.— The Chairman : Are you a shareholder.—Mr. Emmett: No, but lam a retention holder.—The Chairman : Then I am afraid we cannot hear you.—Mr. *John Prescott observed that the Secretary had just stated it was not customary to read minutes. If that was so, it was a very bad custom, and well-regulated societies ought to have them read. (Hear, hear.) The question would, how- ever, come up later on, and he trusted it would be fairly and thoroughly thrashed out. He wished to point out the paragraph on the front page of the report relating to properties in hand, and asked who was responsible for that statement appearing on the balance sheet, because the statement was a falsehood, and he wanted to know who was the authority for inserting it in the balance sheet.—Mr. Liptrott (a manager) said the managers were the authorithy, and he asked Mr. Prescott to prove that it was false. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Prescott proceeded to quote figures from the report and said he could not see how anybody who understood figures at all should allow such a statement to appear in the balance sheet. The Secretary: Mr. Prescott has said something that is not correct; nothing has been handed over to future years, it is altogether a misrepresentation. (Hear, hear.) —Mr. Prescott affirmed that what he had stated was

correct. He would point out that the solicitor's bill was lying over, and also that of Mr. Wood, the auditor, and he would ask them to contradict him, if they could.— Mr. Wood (auditor), admitted that the accounts in ques-

tion had not been paid, but this was because the Special Committee had not completed its work, and he thought it was better that the accounts in connection with it should be held over.—Mr. Farrow stated that until the question he had asked had been answered, he did not see how the accounts could be passed, because they had cer- tain matters to talk about, to know the reason why and wherefore, and if the managers could clear themselves of their duty in tiding over a meeting, which should have been called in two or three months after the appointment of the SpecialCommittee—The Chairman: Mr. Farrow, you are wasting the time of the meeting—Mx. Farrow: Nonsense, nonsense.—An amendment suggesting an addition to the report in regard to the balances was then put to the meeting and was declared lost.—Mr. Prescott : I challenge the vote, and must ask for tellers to be ap- pointed.—Mr. It. Davies (solicitor) said he saw that the amendment was negatived by a very large majority.— The statement of accounts was ultimately adopted.

div.head: SOLICITOR RESIGNS.
div.p: THE SOLICITOR RESIGNS.

Mr. Davies (solicitor to the society) stated that he had ' a statement to make on his own behalf, one which he asked them to believe was made with very great regret. That was that he must ask them to accept his resigna- tion after many years' association with the society. He never came to a meeting lately but there was some diffi- culty or other. At that very moment they were voting a dividend which was earned by properties in hand, but they were not paying the retention holders at all. They were neither paying them principal nor interest. There was a considerable sum of money in the bank, and the managers had asked him to advise them to put it out at interest. He had told them that the retention holders were creditors on the club, and until they were settled with, it would not do to go on carrying on the business of the society. They were not acting illegally, but it was not a healthy state for the society to be in. They were bound to sell the properties in hand, and if they could not sell them to advantage during the next 12 : months, thee never would sell them. He asked them to accept his resignation and that of his firm, because the properties had not been sold, in accordance with his frequently expressed wishes. He was of opinion that the society must turn over a new leaf, or they must get somebody who could see daylight a little clearer than lie could himself.—Mr. H. J. Longtow moved that Mr. Davies be asked to withdraw his resignation.—Mr. Davies said as he and the managers differed upon several points, they could not work satisfactorily, and he thought it better that he. should go.—The Chairman seconded Mr. Longton's motion.—Mr. Davies said before the motion was put he must tell them that he should respectfully decline to occupy the position of solicitor to the society. He differed from the managers, and he did not see how they could work harmoniously. He thanked them for their kind ex.pressions, but at the same time he had a character to maintain, and he felt that they could not go on with that immense amount of property in hand, and he considered now was the time for them to make a fair sale—Mr. Glover moved, as an amendment, that the resignation be referred to the board of new managers.—Mr. Prescott seconded, and it was. earriedi unanimously.
ÜBE SPECIAL coanurnw AND MANAGERS AT LOGGER- HEADS.

The Chairman remarked the minutes of the Special Committee which was appointed at the last annualmeet- ing might now 'fairly come before the meeting. He cauld not say anything to support what had been done by the Committee, and lie should content himself with listening to what they had to say.—Mr. Prescott said he had been deputed to speak on behalf of the Special Com- mittee. Unfortunately, the Committee had not been able' to present to the meeting the report which they had hoped to do. He proceeded to enter into details at ,1 great length of the working of the Committee, and was frequently interrupted, much uproar ensuing at one point. In the result he endeavoured to show that the recommendations of the Committee had been ignored, and that the whole of their labours had been wasted:. He said he never had a more unsatisfactory piece of work to perform, but if theshareholders were satisfied he was.—Mr. Sankey replied at length, and stated that the report of the Special Committee was nit printed because of theerpense which would have been entailed.—Mr.. Glover moved that the report be referred to the new board of management, as it appeared they could get no. f urther that night.—Mr. Sankey said the Committee was incapable of thawing up a report so long as Mr. Prescott was with them.—Mr. Brierley was sorry the discussion had gone on so far, and without any appal*. cut result. After the Committee had sat some time they were told that their proceedings were subject to the ap-. proval of the board of management. To that he objected and refused to meet night after night on those grow:ails. —Mr. Alderson seconded Mr. Glover's proposition,. and it was carried.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.-0/1 Sunday sermons were preached in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Frocisham Bridge, in the morning and evening, by the Rev. J. Finch, of Runcorn, and in the afternoon by the Rev. J. Dyer Bray, of the Union Church, Frodsham. The col- lections realized £4.

UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCEE, FRODSHA.M.—On be- half of the Sunday sehool connected with the above church, two sermons were preached by the Rev. G. A. Wilson,of Halifax.thp services being held in the Wesleyan Chapel, lent to the friends for that purpose. The collec- tions were exceedingly good as compared with previous years, amounting in the whole to £l7 3s. 1.1. id.

LOWTON MINERS.—On Saturday about 500 persons, a large number of whom were colliers, left Lowton (St. Mary's Station) for Southport to take part in the monster miners' demonstration. The trips left about 8 a.m., and the first got back about seven o'clock. Mr. T. T. Hayes, of Leigh, was one of the speakers.
J,XTEST E \VS.
WIEDEMANN v. WALPOLE.

The action of Wiedemann v. Walpole, for breach of promise, has been re-entered for trial, Mr. F. Lucius O'Brien having been engaged to conduct the case for the plaintiff. Further evidence will, it is said, be produced on the next hearing, and eminent counsel retained for the plaintiff.

div.head: CHOLERA.-ALARM IN PARIS.
div.p: CHOLERA.-ALARM IN PARIS.

A Paris telegram states that for the past two days Paris has been suffering from oppreßiive heat, the effects of which in some parts of the town are enh inced by the scarcity of water. The Government se:Jill afraid of an inroad of cholera, as a sum of 100,000 irancs has been appropriated at a Cabinet Council to c irry out precau- tionary measures. FURTHER CESSION OF BR ?USN TERRITORY. PAM& FRIDAY. —The " Figaro " publishes a telegram from London stating that the British Government is dis- posed to cede the Island of Dominica to France in I exchange for the renunciation by the latter of all rights , over the Newfoundland fisheries. THE CESSION OF HELIGOLAND. A "Times" Paris telegram says the "Republique Francaise " publishes a letter from a Hamburg corres- , pondent who has been to Heligoland to feel the pulse of the natives, He catechised the landlord of the hotel, who repudiated any German kinship or sympathies,. deprecated the prospect of Prussian taxation; rule, and conscription, protested against the island being used as small change in an Anglo-German bargain, mid expressed confidence that the British Parliament and people would not allow such an inquity.
THE BARROW ELECTION.

div.head: LORD HARTINGTON'S LETTER.
div.p: LORD HARTINGTON'S LETTER.

A Barrow correspondent yesterday telegraphs :—Last night,when the Liberal Unionists decided to support Mr. Caine they were unaware that a letter had been received by the Conservatives from Lord Hartington opposing Mr. Caine's, candidature. This letter has thrown them into the greatest cimsternatien. The Conservatives are, of course, making the most of the letter, and during the • day will publish it broadcast amongst the electors. As the contest progresses the excitement increases, and the supporters of all the candidates are putting forth every effort. The Conservatives are confident of winning the election? especially after Lord Hartingtores- letter.
CARDINAL MANNING AND MR. CAINE.

Cardinal Manning has addressed a letter to Mr. Caine in which his eminence, referring to licenses, says the contest is distinctly on an issue of morality, and Mr. Caine has put the great issue with fearless courage.

IRISH m.e.'s SUPPORTING MR. DUNCAN. Mr, Conway, M.P., was to speak for Mr. Duncan last night, and Mr. John Dillon will speak on his behalf to- night. Arrangements are being made for a large num- ber of meetings for each of the candidates.

div.head: TIM CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE'S ADDRESS.
div.p: TIM CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE'S ADDRESS.

Mr. H. H. Wainwright, the Conservative candidate, issued his address on Friday morning. He first refers to Mr. Caine's unwillingness to re-enter Parliament as a supporter of the Liberal Unionist party, and says that conscious of the great advantages that have accrued from the statesmanlike policy of the present Government, he is prepared to give it his hearty support. He has always been an advocate of temperance,but cannot support the principles of confiscation. He also expresses willingness to give cordial support to any just measure calculated to improve the social position of the Irish people and to any well- considered measure that will assist a parent in the education of a child. In foreign affairs he is a supporter of Lord Salisbury's policy.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS, YESTERDAY. THE INDIAN ARMY.—The MARQUIS of RIPON called attention to papers relating to army organisation in India, and especially to the recommendation of succes- sive Governments of India in favour of abolition of existing arrangements for the Commander-in-Chief of the Madras and Bombay armies. The Marquis of RrvoN advocated the centralisation of military authority in India. Lord Caosesaid the military authorities were divided in opinion on the subject. The Duke of CAM- BRIDGE thought it would be dangerous to make any sudden, organic change. The subject then dropped. CATTLE DISEASE.—The Contagious Diseases Animals (Pleuro-pneumonia) Bill passed through Committee. THE REWARD OF INVENTION.—IR reply to Lord Sude- ley, Lord ELPHINSTONE said the Treasury would award Admiral Columb £2,000 for hie invention of flashing signals. The House then adjourned.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—YESTERDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. HELIGOLAND,—Mr. PEROT:I96ON, replying LO Sir Robert Fowler, said British rights of fishing in territorial waters of Heligoland would not be retained after the cession to Germany. QtrasrioNs,—Mr. FRaoussos,, replying to Mr. Bryce, said there were no papers of importance to present respecting the conversion of the Egyptian debt.—Mr. Jacitscm, replying to Mr. Bradlaugh, said the memo- rial from the Chambers of Corninerce had been received asking for an extension of customs hours for land- ing and shipping goods. Inquiry would be made. , Mr. FERGI7SSON,, in, reply to Mr. Alfred Pease, said the Government had not accepted the Hinterland doctrine of Germany. The claims of Portugal to African territory rested upon a different basis. Negotiations were still proceeding about the region to-the rear of Walficsh Bay as a sphere of British influence. Replying further to Mr. Cameron,Mr. FERGUSSON said the Government had under- taken no obligation with European powers either in Anglo-German agreement or otherwise. DIVORCE Laws:—Mr. Hunter brought in a Bill to amend the laws of divorce in. England, and it was read the first time. PARLIAMENTARY PROCEDURE.—Mr. Smith moved the appointment of a Select Committee to consider abridged procedure on partly considered bills. Mr. Labouchere moved the omission of the name of Mr. T. W. Russel and insertion of that of Mr. Arthur O'Connor. Mr. SMITFI said lie could not accede to the suggestion. The Government must adhere to the practice since 1830. After some discussion the Committee was appointed as nominated, the amenddient that Mr. ,Arthur O'Connor's name should be substituted far that of Mr. T. W. Russell being rejected by 275 votss. to 163. THE POLICE BILL—The HOME SECRETARY then moved the second reading of the Police Bill, and, in doing so, said the Committee in 1875, which went exhaustively into the question of police superannuation, reported that dissatisfaction existed, especially in provincial forces, mainly on the ground of the uncertainty of pensions, but also on the ground that police constables had to wait until they were invalided or had attaioed sixty years of age before they could receive any pension. The Bill was based on the Bill which was introduced by Sir W. Harcourt in 1885. Its object was twofold. It first proposed to give not only fair but liberal treatment to the constabulary of the country and full consideration to what was fair to ratepayers. [LEFT SITTING.]

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

A monthly meeting of this Council will be held on Tuesday evening next. Amongst the business that will come before it are the matters mentioned below. THE STATE' OF' THE: DRAlNS.—Councillor Muir has given notice that he will ask the following question : " Will the Chairman of of the Paving and sewerage Committee assure this Council and the Burgesses that his Committee will endeavour to obviate the nuisance. arising from stenches in the public streets of the borough, and the dangers to health caused by sewage gas found in private dwellings and other places." THE INFIRMA.I2r EXTENSION.—The Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee will recommend the Council to grant to the Trustees of the Warrington Infirmary a plot of land adjoining the Infirmary, containing about 438' square yards,. according to the amended plan, now ap- proved by the Committee subject to the following:con- ditions :-1. If' the land shall at any time cease to be used for the purposes of the Infirmary, it shall revert to the Corporation;: 2'. The elevation of the buildings front- ing the Park to be approved by the Corporation 3: No unnecessary damage to be done to the trees crr shrubs;; ,4. If it iS fOund necessary to interfere with any build- ings of the Corporation, the Infirmary Committee to re- I 'build or replace such buildings in such manner as• may •be required by the Corporation. It is understood that- the above grant is subject to the approval of the Trea- sury. Mr. Wm. Owen attended the Committee and sub- mitted the plans for the extension of the ,Infirmary,.' which were examined and approved DEPUTATIONS AND DINNERS.—The General Purposes Committee has passed resolutions that the Mayor. Alderman Burgess, and the Borough Tteasurer- be in- structed to attend the meeting of the Council 0 the Association of Municipal Corporations held on the 27th instant ; also, that the Mayor be authorised to attend' the dinner given by the Association of Municipal Corporations held on the 27th instant.

ALARMINW TRAM COLLISION, About eleven o'clock on Saturday night an alarm ing collision occurred in Park-road, St. Helene, be- tween one of the steam tram ears, of the St. Helens and District Tramways Co., and a waggonette containing a party•of colliers and their wives from flaydock. The waggonette elonged to Mr. W. G. Dixon and was driven by a man named George Chesworth. The return journey was being made to tlaydock when the collision occurred. The re- sult was disastrous. The occupants and driver of the waggonette were thrown out, the vehicle was overturned and considerably damaged.. Several of the passengers were severely bruised and shaken but they were able to proceed to their own homes 6 after some delay,

COUNTY OF CHESTER. CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACTS 1878 AND 1886. -- PLEUR 0 PNEUMONIA. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that at a Meeting of the Executive Committee of the Local Authority of the County of Chester, held at the Crewe Arms Hotel. Crewe, in and for the said County, on Thursday, the 19th day of June, 1890, IT WAS ORDERED that from and after the 25th day of June, 1890, the Regulations made on the 14th day of November, 1889, and the 24th day of January, 1890, be Revoked, and that the following REGULATIONS be made under and by virtue of Article 20 of the Animals Order of 1886, prohibiting and regulating the movement of Cattle into the District of the Local Authority of this County from certain Counties or Places in England and Scotland reapec- tively, that is to say :- 1. That from and after the 25th day of June, 1891, the movement of Cattle (except as hereinafter mentioned in Regulation 4) into the District of the Local Authority of the County of Chester, from the Counties or Places hereinafter I mentioned, shall be ABSOLUTELY PROHIBITED until I this order is revoked, viz. Ayrshire Perthshire Aberdeenshire Renfrewshire Dumbartonshire Stirlingshire Edinburghshire Hampshire Fifeshire Hertfordshire Forfarshire Kent Invernesshire Norfolk Kincardineshire Essex Kinrosshire Cumberland Lanarkshire Lancashire Linlithgowshire West Riding of Yorkshire and from the District of any separate Local authority situate within any of each administrative counties. And ALSO from the MUNICIPAL BOROUGH OF HYDE situate within this administrative county., 2. That Cattle which may have been moved or shall hereafter be moved from any of the before-mentioned Counties or Places respectively into any separate Local Authority situate within this County or into any other County. or any separate Local Authority therein, SHALL NOT iitE MOVED into the District of the Local Authority of this County, except upon a license granted by an Inspector of the Local Authority of this County, which License will only be granted. (a) On a declaration made by the Owner of the Cattle or his Agent that such Cattle have been on the premises of such Owner during 56 days immediately preceding the date of the making of the Declara- tion; (b) And also upon the certificate of a duly qualified Veterinary Surgeon that such Cattle are free from Disease. 3. That all Cattle moved into the district of the Local Authority of this County under the foregoing License, shall be at once isolated by the Owner thereof in this County, and kept isolated from any other Cattle for the period of 28 days. and shall not be moved from the premises of such Owner to which they are first moved for the period of 28 days from their arrival thereat. 4. Fat Cattle intended for immediate slaughter may be moved into the district of the Local Authority of this County, from CUMBERLAND. LANCASHIRE. or the WEST RIDING OF YORKSHIRE, en from the District of any separate Local Authority situate within either of such Counties, upon the following conditions, that is to say— (a) On the Certificate of a duly quadfied Veterinary Surgeon that such Cattle are free from disease. 6. That the Cattle moved pursuant to the last regulation shall be slaughtered within three days from their arrival into this District, and shall be kept isolated from any other Cattle not intended to be slaughtered within such period. 6. All Licenses for removal, together with Declarations and Veterinary Surgeon's Certificates, must accompany the Animals therein mentioned while being moved, and be de- livered up to the Police Meer of the County of Chester near- er to the place of their destination by the Owner or his Agent within forty-eight hours after their arrival thereat. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. Chester, 20th June, 1890. NOTES. The foregoing Regulations do not restrict the movement of Animals by Railway through the District of the Local Authority of this County without untrucking. The District of the Local Authority of the County of Chester does not include the City of Chester nor any of the Municipal Boroughs either wholly or partly within this County. "Cattle" means Bulls, Cows, Oxen. Heifers, and Calves. Any offence against the above Regulations is deemed an offence against the Act of 1878, which renders the offender liable to a penalty of not exceeding Twenty Pounds.
